Chapter 7 · 第七章

Building and Scaling Tech Teams组建与扩展技术团队

— PDF p.183 —

Besides building relationships, running one-on-ones, providing feedback, and growing people through delegation—which are the foundational responsibilities of a tech lead to ensure smooth day-to-day team operations—you'll also take on broader team-building responsibilities. These include recruiting new team members, onboarding them effectively, and conducting performance reviews, all while shaping the team's culture and supporting its growth.

除了建立关系、开展一对一面谈、给予反馈、以及通过授权培养人——这些都是技术负责人保障团队日常顺畅运转的基础职责——你还将承担更广泛的团队建设责任。这包括招募新成员、高效地帮他们入职、开展绩效评估，同时塑造团队文化并支持团队成长。

In this chapter, scaling doesn't just refer to growing your team in size; it's also about taking your team to the next level in terms of capability, structure, and effectiveness.

在本章中，“扩展”不仅仅指团队规模的扩大；它还指让团队在能力、结构和效能上迈上新台阶。

I'll share practical guidance on these aspects of the role, drawn from my own experience. You might face these responsibilities sooner than you expect, and being unprepared can slow down your team's momentum or lead to avoidable friction.

我会结合自身经验，分享在这些职责方面的实操指导。你可能比预想更早面对这些责任，而准备不足会拖慢团队的势头，或带来本可避免的摩擦。

I'll also cover three key challenges that often come up when building and scaling tech teams: building an onboarding process from scratch, enabling effective collaboration, and addressing underperformance when it arises.

我还会讨论在组建和扩展技术团队时常见的三个关键挑战：从零搭建入职流程、促成高效协作，以及在绩效不佳出现时加以应对。

These challenges are complex, but they're also solvable, with the right mindset, tools, and systems in place. This chapter aims to give you a starting point to tackle them confidently and proactively as your team grows.

这些挑战虽然复杂，但只要具备正确的心态、工具和体系，它们都是可以解决的。本章旨在给你一个起点，让你随着团队成长，自信而主动地去应对它们。

Recruiting and Onboarding Developers招募新成员并高效入职

The amount of effort you'll need to invest in recruiting and onboarding depends on factors such as the size of your team and the reason for the opening, whether you're building a new team from scratch, scaling an existing one, or backfilling for someone who left. While these tasks might not be part of your day-to-day work, they become a key focus when the need arises.

你在招聘和入职上需要投入多少精力，取决于团队规模以及这个空缺产生的原因——无论你是从零组建新团队、扩展现有团队，还是为离职者补缺。这些工作或许不属于你的日常，但一旦有需求，它们就会成为重点。

— PDF p.184 —

In more established teams, recruitment may come in waves, triggered by new projects, team members leaving, or evolving business needs. Sometimes, the hiring need isn't about growth but about balance, bringing in the right mix of experience levels, skills, and interests to ensure strong team dynamics, well-rounded coverage, and no one being stretched too thin.

在较为成熟的团队中，招聘可能呈波浪式出现，由新项目、成员离职或业务需求变化触发。有时招聘需求并非为了扩张，而是为了平衡——引入经验层级、技能和兴趣的合理搭配，以确保团队化学反应良好、覆盖全面、且没有人被压得过重。

As a tech lead, your level of involvement in hiring depends greatly on your company's size and structure. In some organizations, tech leads are expected to co-own the process alongside engineering managers or internal recruiters. In others, you might simply provide input at key stages, such as designing the technical evaluation or participating in final decision making.

作为技术负责人，你在招聘中的参与程度很大程度上取决于公司的规模和结构。在有些组织里，技术负责人需要与工程经理或内部招聘人员共同主导招聘流程；在另一些组织里，你可能只在关键阶段提供输入，比如设计技术评估环节或参与最终决策。

Even when you're not leading the process end to end, your input remains critical. You're often best positioned to assess a candidate's technical fit for your team's specific work, how well they'll mesh with the team's culture and ways of working, and whether they bring complementary skills or perspectives.

即使你没有从头到尾主导整个流程，你的意见依然至关重要。你往往最有资格判断候选人在技术上是否匹配团队的具体工作、他们能否融入团队文化与工作方式，以及他们能否带来互补的技能或视角。

You may also be asked to help shape or adapt existing hiring processes by refining interview rubrics, identifying gaps in the evaluation loop, or helping to clarify what “good” looks like for a particular role. And while you might not be the one pushing the process forward alone, you'll still need to ensure it aligns with your team's needs and timelines, and that whoever joins is set up to succeed from day one.

你也可能被请去帮助塑造或调整现有招聘流程，比如细化面试评分标准、找出评估环节中的缺口，或帮助明确某个岗位“优秀”长什么样。虽然你或许不是独自推动流程的人，但你仍需确保流程与团队需求和时间表一致，并确保任何加入者从第一天起就被置于能成功的位置。

This section will help you step confidently into this responsibility, covering what to focus on when interviewing and how to design an onboarding process that supports both the new hire and the team as a whole.

本节将帮助你自信地承担起这一责任，涵盖面试时应关注什么，以及如何设计一个既能支持新人、又能支持整个团队的入职流程。

Identifying Team Needs识别团队需求

A balanced team is one that meets the needs of the organization while staying effective and growing sustainably. It's about having a good mix of experience levels: junior developers, mid-level developers, senior developers, and leads (tech leads, staff engineers, principal engineers) so that responsibilities are covered without gaps or overload.

一个均衡的团队，既能满足组织的需求，又能保持高效并可持续成长。它意味着拥有合理搭配的经验层级：初级、中级、高级开发人员，以及负责人（技术负责人、staff 工程师、principal 工程师），从而让职责覆盖既无缺口、也不过载。

When a team lacks this balance, problems start to appear.

当团队缺乏这种平衡时，问题就会开始出现。

Many businesses assume that a team made up entirely of senior engineers and leads will run smoothly with fewer issues. In reality, that setup brings its own challenges. With too much seniority, responsibilities can start to overlap, leading to inefficiencies and, at times, conflicts over ownership. For example, when multiple senior engineers all want to take the lead on a new initiative, it can create competition and friction instead of clear direction. Without clear role distribution, decision making can become slow and contentious, impacting overall team productivity. Everyone can do everything, and everyone is expected to do the same things.

很多公司以为，一个全由高级工程师和负责人组成的团队会运转顺畅、问题更少。实际上，这种配置会带来它自身的挑战。资历过深时，职责会开始重叠，导致效率低下，有时还会在归属权上产生冲突。例如，当多位高级工程师都想在一个新举措中牵头时，这反而会造成竞争和摩擦，而不是清晰的方向。没有明确的角色分工，决策会变得缓慢且充满争议，影响团队整体生产力。结果是谁都能做所有事，而谁又都被期望做同样的事。

— PDF p.185 —

This can go in two directions. One possibility is long conversations and debates whenever a decision needs to be made, as everyone has experience and a strong opinion on how things should be; seniors tend to be particularly opinionated. The other outcome is that some people become unmotivated and hold back their input because they feel there isn't enough space for their voice to be heard.

这会走向两个方向。一种可能是：每当需要做决策时，都会陷入冗长的讨论和辩论，因为每个人都有经验、对事情该怎么做都有强烈主张；资深者尤其固执己见。另一种结果是：有些人变得动力不足、不再发表意见，因为他们觉得没有足够空间让自己的声音被听到。

Also, everyone tends to aim for the same career advancements. Seniors often aspire to move into staff engineer or principal roles, but there are usually limited opportunities for these career advancements. This increased competition can lead to frustration and stagnation, making some individuals feel stuck or demotivated. This means more competition and less opportunities for upscaling. This can quickly demotivate people, causing them to become complacent, stop pushing themselves, or, in some cases, burn out or leave altogether.

此外，大家往往都瞄准同一种晋升路径。资深者常想升到 staff 或 principal 岗位，但这类晋升机会通常有限。竞争加剧会导致挫败和停滞，让一些人觉得被困住或失去动力。这意味着竞争更多、上升空间更少。这会迅速消磨人的干劲，让他们变得自满、不再鞭策自己，甚至在某些情况下倦怠或干脆离开。

There's also the issue of pressure: when everyone is senior, some may hesitate to ask questions they consider basic or challenge their peers, fearing they “should already know this.”

还有压力的问题：当人人都是资深者时，有些人会羞于问自己认为“基础”的问题，或不敢质疑同伴，因为他们担心自己“早该知道这个”。

Junior engineers, on the other hand, bring fresh perspectives. They ask questions that challenge assumptions and encourage rethinking long-standing practices because they want to learn. They might also see activities like cleaning feature toggles as interesting and as an opportunity to learn something new, which will make them prioritize them, making it a win for the whole team, whereas seniors might find it boring. A team without juniors might lose out on this energy and innovation.

另一方面，初级工程师会带来新鲜的视角。他们会提出挑战既有假设的问题，促使大家重新思考长期沿袭的做法，因为他们渴望学习。他们还可能把清理 feature toggle 这类事看作有趣、能学到新东西的机会，从而主动优先处理，这对整个团队都是好事；而资深者可能觉得这很枯燥。一个没有初级成员的团队，可能会失去这种活力和创新。

Another downside to having a team of only very experienced members is the lack of mentorship opportunities. If there are no less experienced devs to mentor, senior engineers miss out on developing leadership skills. I once saw a team where all the engineers were senior-level really struggling to make decisions. While technically strong, they often got stuck debating architectural decisions for too long. When they brought in junior developers, explaining concepts to them forced the seniors to clarify their thinking, leading to faster and better decision making.

全由资深成员组成团队的另一个缺点，是缺乏带教机会。如果没有较 junior 的开发可以指导，高级工程师就错失了培养领导能力的机会。我曾见过一个全是高级工程师的团队，做决策异常艰难。他们技术虽强，却常常在架构决策上争论太久。当他们引入初级开发后，向这些新人解释概念的过程，迫使资深者厘清自己的思路，从而做出更快、更好的决策。

On the other end of the spectrum, a team made up entirely of less experienced engineers faces different struggles. Without experienced team members to learn from, they rely on trial and error, which slows down progress and increases mistakes. This also puts a huge burden on the tech lead, who becomes the only source of guidance. Without additional experienced engineers to help set standards, code quality and architecture will suffer.

而在光谱的另一端，一个全由经验较浅工程师组成的团队则面临不同的困境。没有有经验的成员可以学习，他们只能靠反复试错，这会拖慢进展、增加错误。这也给技术负责人带来巨大负担——他成了唯一的指导来源。没有更多资深工程师帮助设立标准，代码质量和架构都会受损。

— PDF p.186 —

I know a startup that decided to hire only junior engineers to cut costs. While they were enthusiastic and quick learners, they struggled with structuring their codebase efficiently. Without experienced engineers to guide them, they ended up with an overly complex system filled with redundant logic, making maintenance and scaling the business difficult. Eventually, the company had to bring in senior engineers to refactor large parts of the code, costing more time and resources than if they had built a balanced team from the start.

我认识一家创业公司，为了省钱只招初级工程师。他们虽热情、学得快，却难以高效地组织代码库。没有资深工程师指导，最终搞出一个过度复杂、充斥冗余逻辑的系统，让维护和业务扩展都变得困难。最后公司不得不请高级工程师来重构大量代码，花费的时间和资源，比一开始就组建均衡团队还要多。

To build a truly balanced team, you need to think beyond just roles and titles. A balanced team means having a healthy mix of experience levels, skill sets, interests, and motivations. This kind of diversity brings many advantages: broader coverage of your product's needs and greater innovation through varied perspectives.

要打造真正均衡的团队，你需要超越岗位和头衔去思考。均衡的团队意味着在经验层级、技能组合、兴趣和动机上都有健康的搭配。这种多样性带来诸多优势：对产品需求更广泛的覆盖，以及通过多元视角实现更强的创新。

For example, in a full-stack team, some people might prefer frontend work while others are more interested in infrastructure. This balance ensures that different areas of the system get proper attention. This does not mean creating knowledge silos; it's just about having people who will go the extra mile when it comes to that particular topic because they are more interested in it.

例如，在一个全栈团队里，有人可能更喜欢前端工作，有人则对基础设施更感兴趣。这种平衡能确保系统的不同领域都得到应有的关注。这并不是要制造知识孤岛；只是让那些对某个主题更感兴趣的人，愿意在该领域多走一步。

But achieving this balance requires intentionality. Start by asking yourself: What problem am I trying to solve? Are there skill gaps on the team? The good news is that answering these questions and deciding how to move forward is a shared responsibility. You'll work closely with your manager, product managers, and other key stakeholders to make these decisions together and ensure the team is set up to deliver effectively.

但要达成这种平衡需要刻意为之。先问自己：我想解决什么问题？团队里是否存在技能缺口？好消息是，回答这些问题并决定下一步怎么走，是共同的责任。你会与经理、产品经理和其他关键干系人紧密协作，共同做这些决策，确保团队被置于能高效交付的位置。

If the issue is experience, consider whether some of your junior engineers are ready to take on more responsibility. Promoting from within can inject new energy into the team while solving capability gaps. If the issue is a lack of specific technical skills—perhaps your team is about to adopt a new technology that no one is familiar with—this might require hiring externally or temporarily bringing in experts from other teams to share knowledge.

如果问题出在经验上，不妨看看你的初级工程师里是否有人已准备好承担更多责任。内部晋升既能为团队注入新活力，又能补上能力缺口。如果问题是缺乏特定技术技能——比如团队即将采用一门无人熟悉的新技术——那可能需要外部招聘，或临时从其他团队请专家来分享知识。

Don't just default to thinking, “I need two more seniors.” Instead, reframe the question: “What outcomes are we missing because of the current imbalance?” Maybe the team is too quiet and lacks fresh perspectives. In that case, bringing in enthusiastic junior talent can help. Or maybe the team debates endlessly without clear decisions, pointing to a need for stronger leadership or clarity.

不要默认就想“我还需要两个资深的”。相反，把问题换个提法：“因为当前的不平衡，我们正在错失哪些成果？”也许团队过于安静、缺乏新鲜视角，那样的话引入热情的初级人才会有帮助。又或者团队无休止地争论、却迟迟做不出清晰决策，这就指向需要更强的领导力或更清晰的方向。

— PDF p.187 —

Also, keep in mind that every team is different. They're at different stages of growth and have unique challenges. When joining or starting a new team, the key is to assess where they are right now and what's holding them back. Once you understand that, you can decide whether the answer is promotion, hiring, restructuring, or something else.

还要记住，每个团队都不一样。它们处于不同的成长阶段，面临独特的挑战。加入或组建新团队时，关键是评估它现在处于什么位置、是什么在拖它后腿。一旦弄清这些，你就能判断答案是晋升、招聘、重组，还是别的什么。

The best part of a well-balanced team is that it creates a strong learning culture. Juniors have mentors to guide them. Seniors and leads get leadership opportunities. The tech lead can focus on strategy instead of being the sole source of knowledge. And with diverse perspectives in the mix, the team becomes better at solving problems and thinking critically about its work.

一个均衡团队最棒的地方在于，它会造就浓厚的学习文化。初级者有导师指引，资深者和负责人获得领导机会，技术负责人能专注于战略、而不是充当唯一的知识来源。再加上多元视角的融合，团队会更善于解决问题、更善于对自己的工作进行批判性思考。

Effective Recruiting and Interviewing Strategies高效的招聘与面试策略

At some point as a tech lead, you'll find yourself hiring people for your team. The level of your involvement may vary depending on the company, but you should at least be aware of the process and know what to expect. Here are some strategies that can help you recruit and interview tech candidates more effectively:

作为技术负责人，到某个阶段你就会开始为团队招人。你的参与程度因公司而异，但你至少应该了解流程、知道会发生什么。以下是一些能帮你更有效地招募和面试技术候选人的策略：

Get clear on why you're hiring先想清楚你为什么招人

You might think, “Obviously, we need more people.” But take a moment to get specific. Are you hiring because someone left and there's a team size quota? Because you're starting a new initiative and need to build a team from scratch? Because you're overloaded with work and the current team can't keep up? Or maybe you're missing a key skill set or trying to rebalance your team across experience levels? The answer to this question shapes everything: how you interview, what you look for, and how the new hire will integrate. I've seen engineers struggle when they join a team with vague expectations. And when that's the case, guess who they turn to for clarity? You. That lack of alignment not only frustrates them but slows everyone else down.

你可能会想：“这不明摆着嘛，我们需要更多人。”但请花点时间说得更具体些。你招人是因为有人离职、要补团队编制？因为要启动一个新举措、得从零搭团队？因为工作过载、现有团队跟不上？还是因为缺少某项关键技能，或想在经验层级上重新平衡团队？这个问题的答案决定了一切：你如何面试、你看重什么、新人将如何融入。我见过工程师加入一个期望模糊的团队后很挣扎。而这种时候，你猜他们会找谁去问清楚？找你。这种对齐的缺失不仅让他们沮丧，也拖慢了其他所有人。

When you're clear on why you're hiring, it becomes much easier to answer that common interview question: “How will I contribute to the team?”

当你清楚自己为什么招人时，就更容易回答面试中那个常见问题：“我将如何为团队做贡献？”

Get clarity on the whole process搞清楚整个流程

Even if you're not involved in every step of the hiring process, it's incredibly useful to understand the full journey a candidate goes through. Before jumping into interviews, take some time to familiarize yourself with the entire flow. Look for any documented processes and have a check-in with the HR person responsible for the process and work closely with this person to understand what each stage looks like, where you fit in and what's expected of you, how you will track candidates and feedback, and how you will collaborate during the process. To get even more context, jump into a quick conversation with another tech lead who's been part of recent hiring rounds.

即使你不参与招聘流程的每一步，了解候选人经历的完整旅程也非常有用。在开始面试之前，花点时间熟悉整个流程。找找有没有成文的流程，并与负责该流程的 HR 聊一聊、紧密协作，弄清楚每个阶段长什么样、你在其中处于什么位置、对你的期望是什么、你将如何跟踪候选人和反馈、以及流程中如何协作。为了获得更多背景，再找一位近期参与过招聘的技术负责人快速聊一聊。

This broader view will help you prepare for candidate questions, and the close collaboration with HR will make the process smoother on all sides but also might trigger some ideas for improvement of the overall process.

这种更全局的视角会帮你更好地准备候选人的提问；而与 HR 的紧密协作不仅会让流程各方都更顺畅，还可能触发你对整体流程改进的一些想法。

— PDF p.188 —

Write a job description that reflects reality写出贴近现实的岗位描述

Sometimes you get a boilerplate job description handed down from HR or a company-wide template. If you are interviewing for your team and can influence or adjust it, absolutely do it. Add context that's specific to your team. What problem are you solving? What stage is your team at? What kind of collaboration do you expect: do you pair regularly, do you work async, are there on-call rotations? What are the must-have technical skills and the nice-to-haves? When candidates understand the real picture, you attract people who are both more qualified and more enthusiastic about your specific context, not just “a backend role somewhere.”

有时你拿到的是 HR 下发的模板化岗位描述，或全公司通用的模板。如果你在为自己的团队面试、并且能影响或调整它，那就一定要去做。加入你团队特有的背景。你们在解决什么问题？团队处于什么阶段？你期望怎样的协作方式：经常结对吗？异步办公吗？有 on-call 轮值吗？哪些技术技能是必须的、哪些是加分项？当候选人了解真实情况时，你吸引来的人会既更胜任、又对你具体的上下文更有热情，而不是只冲着“某处的一个后端岗位”而来。

Even if you're conducting interviews that aren't directly for your team, like contributing to a company-wide hiring pipeline or helping out another team, don't overlook opportunities to improve the process. If you notice something that could be better, share your feedback with HR or the hiring coordinator. Whether it's a gap in the interview loop, unclear evaluation criteria, or a misalignment between job descriptions and reality, your input can make a big difference. Improving the hiring process benefits not just your team but the entire organization.

即使你面试的岗位不是直接面向自己团队的——比如为全公司的招聘管线出力、或帮别的团队——也不要忽略改进流程的机会。如果你注意到什么可以做得更好，就把反馈告诉 HR 或招聘协调人。无论是面试环节的缺口、不清晰的评估标准，还是岗位描述与现实不符，你的意见都能带来很大改变。改进招聘流程不仅惠及你的团队，也惠及整个组织。

Make the process inclusive (on purpose)（有意识地）让流程具备包容性

Inclusion doesn't start in the interview room. It begins with the job description and runs through every step of the hiring process.

包容并非从面试间才开始。它始于岗位描述，并贯穿招聘流程的每一步。

Even small details, like how you write a job ad, can influence who applies. Certain phrases or tone choices can unintentionally discourage women or underrepresented candidates from applying.

即便是一些小细节，比如你写招聘广告的措辞，也会影响谁来应聘。某些措辞或语气，可能在无意中让女性或代表性不足的候选人却步。

— PDF p.189 —

Interview format matters too. A two-hour whiteboard session in front of multiple interviewers might feel standard to some but intimidating or exclusionary to others. That's why flexibility matters.

面试形式也很重要。在多位面试官面前进行两小时白板答题，对某些人来说稀松平常，对另一些人却可能令人生畏、甚至有排斥感。这就是为什么灵活性很重要。

Ideally, your process offers a few different options and adapts to the needs of individual candidates. For example, someone with caregiving responsibilities might prefer the flexibility of a take-home task. Take-home tests, pair programming sessions, and async exercises all have their pros and cons, and no one format works for everyone.

理想情况下，你的流程会提供几种不同选项，并根据候选人个人的需求灵活调整。例如，有照护家人责任的人可能更喜欢居家任务的灵活性。居家测试、结对编程、异步练习各有优缺点，没有一种形式适用于所有人。

That said, adapting the process to each candidate takes coordination and effort. It requires alignment across the hiring team and more flexibility in scheduling, which is why only a handful of tech companies have been experimenting with this kind of customization so far.

话虽如此，为每位候选人调整流程需要协调和精力。它要求招聘团队达成一致，并在排期上更灵活，这也是为什么迄今只有少数科技公司在尝试这种定制化。

But even if you can't offer this level of flexibility just yet, it's worth rethinking your current approach. Instead of sticking with “This is how we've always done it,” start small. Test changes. Pay attention to the candidate experience.

但即使你暂时还做不到这种程度的灵活，也值得重新审视现有做法。不要抱着“我们一直就是这么做的”不放，而是从小处着手。试点改动。关注候选人的体验。

Also, you can only hire a diverse team if you're starting with one. Homogeneous teams tend to hire in their own image, even unintentionally. If your interview panel lacks diversity, try borrowing interviewers from other teams or departments, especially those who can bring different perspectives. You can also introduce external tools to help reduce implicit bias in your filtering and evaluation process. Injecting diverse voices into hiring decisions at every stage makes it far more likely you'll build a team that reflects a broader range of experiences and ideas.

此外，只有当你本身就拥有一个多元的团队，才可能招到多元的团队。同质化的团队往往会照着自己的样子招人，哪怕并非有意。如果你的面试小组缺乏多样性，不妨从其他团队或部门借调面试官，尤其是那些能带来不同视角的人。你也可以引入外部工具，帮助在筛选和评估环节减少隐性偏见。在招聘决策的每个阶段注入多元声音，会大大提高你建成一个反映更广泛经历与想法的团队的概率。

Your hiring process should aim to get the best out of each candidate by creating a fair, inclusive environment that mirrors the actual work of the role, without introducing unnecessary barriers.

你的招聘流程应当通过营造公平、包容、且能真实反映岗位工作的环境，让每位候选人发挥出最佳水平，而不设置不必要的障碍。

Keep an open mind when interviewing面试时保持开放心态

We all carry biases, even if we don't realize it. It's very natural to gravitate toward people who share your background, your interests, your career path. But that mindset can really narrow your field of view. You risk overlooking someone who could bring fresh ideas, different experiences, or complementary skills to your team. Not only that, but you slow down the process because your bar becomes too specific.

我们每个人都带有偏见，哪怕自己没有意识到。人会本能地被那些与自己背景、兴趣、职业道路相似的人吸引，这非常自然。但这种心态确实会窄化你的视野。你有可能错过一个本可为团队带来新鲜想法、不同经历或互补技能的人。不仅如此，当你的标尺变得过于具体，你还会拖慢整个流程。

The best teams aren't made up of clones; they're made up of people who cover each other's gaps. So when you're interviewing, pause and reflect on what you're actually evaluating. Are you looking for familiarity, or for someone who could challenge your assumptions in a good way?

最优秀的团队不是由一个个复制品组成的，而是由能互相补位的人组成的。所以面试时，请停下来反思你究竟在评估什么。你是在寻找熟悉感，还是在寻找一个能以有益的方式挑战你既有假设的人？

— PDF p.190 —

Involve the whole team让整个团队参与进来

Hiring shouldn't rest solely on your shoulders. The team will work with the new person, so they should share responsibility in choosing them. That shared ownership often leads to better hires and a stronger team culture overall.

招聘不应只压在你一个人肩上。团队将与新人共事，因此他们应当共同承担挑选新人的责任。这种共同拥有权往往会带来更好的招聘结果和更强的团队文化。

Involving the team doesn't mean the candidate needs to meet every single person during interviews. But everyone should have a chance to contribute to the process. That might mean helping draft the job description, participating in technical interviews, or leading culture interviews.

让团队参与，并不意味着候选人需要在面试中见到每一个人。但每个人都应有机会为流程出力。这可能是帮着起草岗位描述、参与技术面试，或主导文化匹配面试。

A common trap is letting only the tech lead or senior engineers handle interviews, which misses out on a bunch of benefits. When more people are involved, you can run interviews faster and avoid bottlenecks.

一个常见的陷阱是只让技术负责人或高级工程师来做面试，这会错失诸多好处。当更多人参与进来，你可以更快地安排面试、避免瓶颈。

It's also a growth opportunity. Interviewing builds soft skills like asking thoughtful questions, really listening, and clearly explaining complex ideas. Plus, more voices mean a better chance of spotting whether someone is a good culture fit. And from the candidate's side, it makes the process feel more authentic, as they're not just meeting the leadership; they're meeting the team they might actually work with.

这同时也是一个成长机会。面试能锻炼软技能，比如提出有深度的问题、真正地倾听、以及清晰地解释复杂的想法。此外，更多的声音意味着更有可能判断某人是否契合团队文化。而从候选人的角度看，这会让流程显得更真实——他们见到的不只是领导层，还有将来真正要一起共事的团队。

Constantly improve as an interviewer持续提升自己的面试能力

Interviewing is a skill like any other. Just because you're expected to jump into it doesn't mean you're instantly good at it. And that's totally OK. Start small. Reflect after each interview: Did the conversation flow naturally? Did you find yourself repeating questions or running out of time? Were there moments where you weren't sure what to ask next? Talk to someone with more interviewing experience and bounce your challenges off them. Ask how they would approach the situations you found tricky.

面试和其他技能一样，是一门需要修炼的手艺。公司指望你上手，并不代表你一开始就擅长。这完全正常。从小处做起。每次面试后复盘：对话顺畅吗？你是否发现自己在重复提问、或时间不够用？有没有某些瞬间你不知道接下来该问什么？找一位面试经验更丰富的人聊聊，把你遇到的挑战抛给他们。问问他们会如何处理你觉得棘手的那些情形。

If you're pairing during interviews, like we used to do at Thoughtworks, take advantage of that setup. Ask your partner for feedback. Did they notice anything you could do differently next time?

如果你在面试时是搭档进行的——就像我们当年在 Thoughtworks 那样——好好利用这种安排。向搭档征求反馈。他们有没有注意到你下次可以改进的地方？

And don't forget the most direct source of feedback: the candidate. While this might be new for your company, or not part of the default process, it's worth exploring. Sometimes it requires building a stronger relationship with HR or recruiting so that feedback isn't filtered or lost. Hearing how the interview experience felt from the candidate's side can uncover blind spots and help you improve faster.

也别忘了最直接的反馈来源：候选人。虽然这对你的公司可能是新鲜事、或不是默认流程的一部分，但值得一试。有时这需要与 HR 或招聘团队建立更牢固的关系，以免反馈被过滤或丢失。听听候选人那边对面试体验的真实感受，能暴露你的盲点，帮你更快进步。

— PDF p.191 —

Improving your interview skills is good for your team and for you. The more prepared and confident you become, the less stressful and more effective interviews will feel.

提升面试能力，对团队和你自己都有好处。你准备得越充分、越自信，面试就会越轻松、越高效。

Get involved in sourcing candidates主动参与候选人寻访

It's easy for tech leads to take a backseat when it comes to sourcing, assuming it's entirely the recruiting team's job. But you can have a real impact here, and the earlier you get involved, the more influence you have over the type of candidates coming through the pipeline.

在寻访候选人这件事上，技术负责人很容易退居幕后，以为这完全是招聘团队的活。但你其实可以在这里产生真正的影响；而且你介入得越早，对进入招聘管线的候选人类型就越有话语权。

Start by thinking about your own network. Are there people you've worked with before or know from the community who might be a good fit? Reach out. Be vocal about hiring when you attend meetups or industry events. A simple post on LinkedIn sharing what your team is working on can go a long way.

先从你自己的人脉想起。有没有你以前共事过、或在技术社区认识、可能合适的人？主动联系。参加线下聚会或行业活动时，大方地对外说你们在招人。在 LinkedIn 上发一条简单的动态、分享团队正在做什么，就能带来很大效果。

You can also help by reviewing inbound applications more intentionally, flagging promising candidates early on, or sharing feedback to refine the sourcing criteria.

你还可以更有针对性地筛选主动投递的简历、尽早标记有潜力的候选人，或分享反馈以优化寻访标准。

The more you engage, the better the odds you'll attract people who are genuinely excited about your team and the problems you're solving.

你参与得越多，就越有可能吸引到真正对你的团队和你们正在解决的问题充满热情的人。

The more you invest in the hiring process, from sourcing to interviews to team involvement, the more you reduce the risk of hiring the wrong fit and having to go through the whole thing again. Being intentional up front saves you a lot of time, energy, and disruption down the line.

你在招聘流程上投入得越多——从寻访、面试到团队参与——就越能降低招错人、再把整个流程重来一遍的风险。前期多一分用心，就能在日后省下大量时间、精力和反复折腾。

Onboarding Effectively高效入职

A smooth onboarding process is a key part of a high-performing team and will have a great impact on your overall team success. A well-structured onboarding process enables new hires to ramp up quickly, work autonomously, and feel like valuable contributors from day one. It ensures they gain mastery over their daily tasks and develop a solid understanding of the team's history, expectations, and ways of working. Yet, it's often treated as an afterthought in tech teams, leading to unnecessary confusion and frustration.

顺畅的入职流程是高绩效团队的关键组成部分，会对团队整体成功产生重大影响。结构良好的入职流程能让新人快速上手、独立工作，并从第一天起就感到自己是有价值的贡献者。它确保新人熟练掌握日常任务，并对团队的历史、期望和工作方式形成扎实的理解。然而，在技术团队里它却常常被当作事后补做的事，导致本可避免的困惑和挫败。

I've seen people leave companies because of a poor onboarding experience. A staff engineer once joined a large tech company only to find no clear documentation, no connections between systems, and no defined expectations for her role, leaving her frustrated and unsupported. Six months later, she left. And she's not alone. Many companies underestimate how critical those first few months are for retention and productivity.

我见过有人因为糟糕的入职体验而离职。有位 staff 工程师加入一家大型科技公司后，却发现没有清晰的文档、系统之间没有关联、对她的角色也没有明确期望，让她倍感挫败、孤立无援。六个月后她离职了。而且她并非个例。很多公司都低估了最初几个月对留人与产能的关键作用。

— PDF p.192 —

Given the fast-changing nature of the tech industry, ensuring new joiners ramp up quickly and contribute effectively has never been more important. A great onboarding process means guiding new hires through a structured, engaging experience that helps them integrate smoothly, rather than simply overwhelming them with documentation.

鉴于科技行业瞬息万变，确保新人快速上手、高效贡献，其重要性前所未有。一个好的入职流程，是引导新人经历一段结构化、有参与感的体验，帮助他们顺利融入，而不是简单地用一堆文档把他们淹没。

The best onboarding experiences share common characteristics. They are intentional, structured, and involve the whole team. In the following sections, we'll go over what they look like in practice.

最好的入职体验有一些共同特征：它们是刻意设计的、结构化的，并且让整个团队都参与其中。在接下来的小节里，我们会看看它们在实践中长什么样。

Start onboarding before day one在第一天之前就开始入职

Onboarding begins the moment an offer is accepted. A simple welcome email with practical details, like what to expect on the first day, an agenda, and key contacts, sets the tone. For remote employees, laptops and other equipment should arrive before their start date. For in-office hires, everything from desk setups to system access should be ready. Account setups should be completed in advance, or at the very least, there should be a clear process for requesting access to essential tools, so new hires aren't stuck waiting during their first few days.

从 offer 被接受的那一刻起，入职就已经开始了。一封简单的欢迎邮件，附上实用信息——比如第一天会发生什么、日程安排、关键联系人——就定下了基调。对于远程员工，笔记本电脑和其他设备应在入职日前寄达。对于坐班的新人，从工位布置到系统权限都应准备就绪。账号配置应提前完成；至少，也要有一套清晰的申请关键工具权限的流程，免得新人在头几天里干等着。

While these tasks may technically fall under other departments, it's still valuable for tech leads to be aware of the pre-day-one experience. It directly impacts how a new hire shows up on their first day: whether they feel confident, welcomed, and ready to contribute or confused and disconnected.

虽然这些任务严格来说属于其他部门，但技术负责人了解入职前的这段体验依然很有价值。它直接影响新人第一天的状态：是自信、受欢迎、准备好贡献，还是困惑、疏离。

If you notice gaps in this early process, don't hesitate to offer feedback or collaborate with the relevant teams to improve it. Even small improvements here can make a big difference in how smoothly onboarding begins. One simple but effective step you can own: keep a checklist of the essential tools, systems, and services your new team member will need in their first weeks. This gives you a quick way to double-check readiness and, if something is missing, helps you guide the new hire to the right people who can unblock them.

如果你注意到这段早期流程有缺口，不妨主动提供反馈、或与相关团队协作去改进它。这里哪怕很小的改进，也能让入职的开端顺畅很多。有一个简单而有效、可以由你亲自负责的步骤：保留一份清单，列出新成员在头几周需要用到的关键工具、系统和服务。这让你能快速复核准备是否就绪；若有缺漏，也能帮新人找到能为他们解除阻塞的人。

Involve the whole team让整个团队参与进来

As a tech lead, you don't have to do all of this yourself; you just need to make sure it gets done.

作为技术负责人，你不必事必躬亲；你只需要确保这些事被完成。

Too often, I see tech leads taking on the full burden of onboarding, preparing sessions, answering every question, and trying to manage it all alone. Not only does this overwhelm you, but it also robs your team of mentoring opportunities and fresh perspectives on improving the onboarding process. When only one person owns onboarding, it reflects a single viewpoint, and we all know that can be limiting. It's a great opportunity to delegate (you can find the whole delegation process in Chapter 6).

我经常看到技术负责人把入职的全部重担扛在自己身上：准备各种分享会、回答每一个问题、试图独自包揽一切。这不仅会压垮你，还会剥夺团队带教的机会、以及改进入职流程的新鲜视角。当入职只由一个人负责时，它反映的只是单一视角，而我们都知道这是有局限的。这是授权的好机会（完整的授权流程见第 6 章）。

— PDF p.193 —

A common approach is assigning a buddy to the new joiner from day one until onboarding is complete. A buddy is typically a peer, often on the same team, making the process more personal and helping to fill in any gaps. They take ownership of onboarding tasks, plan sessions, and provide day-to-day guidance. Being an onboarding buddy gives new hires the support they need, and at the same time, it offers engineers a valuable opportunity to grow professionally.

一个常见做法是，从第一天起就为新人配一位 buddy（伙伴），直到入职完成。buddy 通常是一位同侪、往往就在同一个团队，让这个过程更有人情味、并帮忙补上各种缺口。buddy 负责入职任务、安排分享会、提供日常指导。做入职 buddy 既给了新人所需的支持，同时也为工程师提供了宝贵的职业成长机会。

While a buddy can deliver all the onboarding sessions, I prefer involving the whole team. In my teams, we split onboarding topics among different members: high-level product overview, architecture, path to production, coding environment setup, ways of working, and team values. Each person prepared documentation, shared it with the team for feedback, and updated it accordingly before presenting it to the new joiner. Even the product owner was part of the process. This not only helped the new joiner meet the team and start building relationships but also encouraged shared ownership of onboarding.

虽然 buddy 可以包揽所有入职分享会，但我更倾向于让整个团队参与。在我的团队里，我们把入职主题分给不同成员：产品概览、架构、发布到生产的路径、编码环境搭建、工作方式、团队价值观。每个人都先准备文档、发给团队征求反馈、据此更新，然后再讲给新人听。就连产品负责人也参与其中。这不仅帮新人认识团队、开始建立关系，也促成了入职这件事的共同拥有。

As a tech lead, make sure the buddy has time to prepare and support onboarding. Expect that their usual workload will be reduced for the first few weeks as they focus on helping the new joiner settle in.

作为技术负责人，要确保 buddy 有时间准备和支持入职。要预期他们在头几周的常规工作量会减少，因为他们要专注帮新人安顿下来。

Another way to involve the team in the onboarding process is to have them pair on tasks with the new joiner. Pairing is one of the fastest ways to get a new joiner up to speed and integrated into the team. These sessions naturally become mini knowledge exchanges, as they help the new joiner explore the codebase, understand past decisions, and learn any quirks in the tooling. The best part is that no extra preparation is needed, just a task to work on and time to collaborate.

让团队参与入职的另一种方式，是让大家与新人结对完成任务。结对是让新人快速上手、融入团队最快的方式之一。这些结对过程自然变成了一场场小型知识交流，帮新人探索代码库、理解过去的决策、了解工具链中的各种 quirks。最棒的是，这不需要额外准备，只要有一个可做的任务和协作的时间即可。

Define a clear plan with actionable steps制定一份带可执行步骤的清晰计划

A well-structured onboarding process includes a clear plan with actionable steps to help new joiners ramp up quickly. In the first few days, they should get an overview of essential topics, from how the company operates to the tools they'll use to ship code.

结构良好的入职流程，应包含一份带可执行步骤的清晰计划，帮新人快速上手。在头几天里，他们应了解一系列关键主题的概览——从公司如何运作，到他们用来发布代码的工具。

A good onboarding schedule includes several key sessions:

一份好的入职日程包含几个关键环节：

  • Company values and mission — Understanding the broader vision公司价值观与使命 —— 理解更宏大的愿景
  • Team ways of working — How the team collaborates and communicates团队工作方式 —— 团队如何协作与沟通
  • Product definition — The team's role within the company and its impact产品定位 —— 团队在公司中的角色及其影响
  • What the team is building and why — The purpose and goals behind their work团队在构建什么、为什么 —— 工作背后的目的与目标
— PDF p.194 —

Many teams skip these high-level sessions and jump straight into technical details, but this foundational knowledge is crucial. Once the big picture is covered, onboarding should move into a few key areas:

很多团队跳过这些高层环节、直接钻进技术细节，但这种基础性知识至关重要。大局观讲完之后，入职应转入几个关键领域：

  • Architecture overview — How the system is structured架构概览 —— 系统是如何组织的
  • Path to production — Steps to deploy code successfully发布到生产的路径 —— 成功部署代码的步骤
  • Pairing sessions — Hands-on guidance for setting up the development environment结对环节 —— 手把手指导搭建开发环境

To support these meetings, provide documentation that new hires can reference later, including the following:

为配合这些会议，提供新人日后可以查阅的文档，包括：

  • Architecture diagrams — A visual representation of the system架构图 —— 系统的可视化表达
  • Path to production guide — A step-by-step breakdown of deployments发布路径指南 —— 部署的分步拆解
  • Product documentation — Key details about what the team is building产品文档 —— 团队在构建之物的关键细节
  • Tooling overview — The technologies and platforms used工具概览 —— 所使用的技术与平台
  • Setup instructions — How to configure their local environment and access essential tools搭建说明 —— 如何配置本地环境并访问关键工具

This documentation can quickly become outdated. Maintaining accurate, up-to-date docs requires discipline, but when it's treated as a shared team responsibility, the effort becomes much more manageable. And this is one of the few types of documentation truly worth investing in keeping up-to-date, as it has a direct impact on how quickly and smoothly new team members can get up to speed.

这些文档很容易过时。维护准确、最新的文档需要自律，但当它被当作团队共同的责任时，这份努力就好承担得多。而且，这是少数几种真正值得投入精力保持更新的文档之一，因为它直接影响新成员上手的速度和顺畅程度。

— PDF p.195 —

Having a structured onboarding guide ensures new joiners have all the information they need to become productive quickly.

有一份结构化的入职指南，能确保新人拥有快速产出所需的全部信息。

Track progress跟踪进展

Onboarding is a team effort, and tracking progress should reflect that. My approach is to create a task on the main team board, assigning both the new joiner and their buddy as owners. This makes onboarding visible and ensures shared responsibility. After all, it affects the whole team and our delivery; even if a buddy has been assigned, it's not just one person's job.

入职是团队的共同努力，跟踪进展也应体现这一点。我的做法是在团队主看板上建一个任务，把新人和他的 buddy 都设为负责人。这让入职变得可见，并确保责任共担。毕竟，它影响整个团队和我们的交付；即便已经指派了 buddy，这也不只是某一个人的事。

By having this task on the board, the new joiner is included in the team's workflow from day one. They have a task to track, give updates on, and, most importantly, use as a way to raise blockers in standups. As we all know, it can be intimidating for a new hire to speak up and ask for help. This setup makes it easier and encourages them to engage early.

把这个任务放在看板上，新人从第一天起就被纳入团队的工作流。他们有一个任务可以跟踪、可以同步进展，最重要的是，可以在站会上借此提出阻塞。我们都知道，新人开口求助可能会有压力。这种安排让它变得更容易，并鼓励他们尽早参与进来。

Another benefit is that it immediately gives them a sense of contribution. Talking about onboarding in stand-ups reinforces that they're part of the team and helps them build confidence as they navigate their first few weeks.

另一个好处是，它立刻给他们一种贡献感。在站会上谈论入职进展，会不断强化“他们是团队一员”这一点，并在他们摸索头几周的过程中帮他们建立信心。

Continuously improve持续改进

You can't improve what you don't measure. Without tracking the impact of changes, you won't know if your onboarding process is actually getting better or making things worse.

你无法改进你不去衡量的东西。不跟踪改动的影响，你就无从知道入职流程究竟是在变好、还是在变糟。

Some teams track onboarding efficiency by measuring how quickly a new hire starts contributing to the codebase. For instance, getting a pull request merged in the first week can signal a few positive things: a solid CI/CD system with guardrails, a culture of frequent iteration, a fast-moving organization, and a practical onboarding process that gets people working quickly.

有些团队通过衡量新人多快开始为代码库做贡献，来跟踪入职效率。例如，第一周就有一个 pull request 被合并，可能意味着几件好事：有一套带护栏的扎实 CI/CD 系统、频繁迭代的文化、快速运转的组织，以及一套能让人迅速进入工作的务实入职流程。

In fact, some teams go as far as encouraging new hires to ship code to production on their very first day. And while this is a popular idea in tech circles, I'm personally not a big fan.

事实上，有些团队甚至鼓励新人第一天就把代码发布到生产环境。虽然这在技术圈里很流行，但我个人并不太认同。

Shipping something on day one can demonstrate maturity in your systems and processes, but it's not always the best experience for the person doing it. For some, it's an exciting challenge. For others, it creates pressure and sends the wrong message, like that speed is more important than integrating in the team or understanding the context.

第一天就发布东西，确实能彰显系统和流程的成熟度，但对当事人来说未必是最好的体验。对有些人，这是令人兴奋的挑战；对另一些人，这会制造压力、传递错误信号——仿佛速度比融入团队、理解上下文更重要。

There are easier, lower-pressure ways to introduce someone to the codebase, like pairing or helping them set up their environment.

要把一个人引入代码库，有更轻松、压力更小的方式，比如结对、或帮他们搭建环境。

— PDF p.196 —

One practice I often encourage is giving new joiners full access to update onboarding documentation, especially setup guides. These are typically the first things to become outdated as tools evolve. Some teams hesitate to allow this, worrying that someone without full context might make incorrect edits. But who better to spot unclear steps than someone going through the process for the first time? It's a chance to make the process clearer and give them an immediate sense of ownership and involvement. If you're concerned about accuracy, simply ask their onboarding buddy or a more experienced team member to review changes before they're finalized.

我常鼓励的一个做法，是给新人完整权限去更新入职文档，尤其是环境搭建指南。随着工具演进，这些往往是最先过时的东西。有些团队对此犹豫，担心缺乏完整上下文的人会改出错误。但还有谁能比第一次走这个流程的人更能发现那些讲不清楚的步骤呢？这既是让流程更清晰的机会，也能让他们立刻产生归属感和参与感。如果你担心准确性，只需请他们的 buddy 或更资深的成员在改动定稿前 review 一下即可。

Of course, just because someone pushes code doesn't mean they're fully onboarded. They still need to meet the team, understand the product and its purpose, get to know the system, and learn how the team works.

当然，一个人提交了代码，并不代表他已经完全入职。他仍需要认识团队、理解产品及其目的、熟悉系统、并学会团队如何协作。

That's why I prefer other metrics for tracking onboarding efficiency: ones that reflect the full experience.

因此，我更倾向于用其他指标来跟踪入职效率：那些能反映完整体验的指标。

For example, you can track the time it takes to complete an onboarding checklist: attending onboarding sessions, gaining access, reading the starting documentation, and setting up the development environment.

例如，你可以跟踪完成一份入职清单所需的时间：参加入职分享会、开通权限、阅读入门文档、搭建开发环境。

Others use lightweight surveys or informal conversations to gather feedback. Was the experience smooth or frustrating? Did they feel supported? Whether or not this is your primary metric, I highly recommend building in feedback loops. Ask new hires to note what felt confusing or missing while the experience is still fresh.

另一些团队用轻量问卷或非正式交流来收集反馈。这段体验是顺畅还是令人挫败？他们感到被支持了吗？无论这是否是你的主要指标，我都强烈建议把反馈闭环建起来。趁体验还新鲜时，请新人记下哪些地方令人困惑、哪些有所缺失。

The key takeaway: there's no one-size-fits-all metric. What matters is that you're tracking something. Whether it's checklist progress, feedback, or something else, choose a signal that fits your team and use it to learn and improve.

关键启示是：没有放之四海而皆准的指标。重要的是你确实在跟踪点什么。无论是清单进度、反馈，还是别的什么，选一个适合你团队的信号，并用它来学习和改进。

Because the real issue is that many teams don't track onboarding at all. They simply assume “it'll get done when it's done,” leaving them with no way to estimate its impact on the team, delivery timelines, or overall efficiency.

因为真正的问题在于：很多团队根本不跟踪入职。他们只是默认“到时候自然就弄完了”，结果无从评估入职对团队、交付时间表或整体效率的影响。

The goal is to recognize onboarding as a system worth improving, then gather feedback, measure progress, and iterate on it continuously.

目标是把入职视为一个值得改进的系统，然后收集反馈、衡量进展、并持续迭代。

Building a High-Performing Team打造高绩效团队

Having, or better said, leading a high-performing team is the ultimate proof of a great tech lead. It's every tech lead's dream to have a team that enjoys working together, feels motivated about what they're building, and runs like a well-oiled machine. A team that's seen as reliable, efficient, and capable of consistently delivering impact.

拥有、或者更准确地说，带领一支高绩效团队，是一位优秀技术负责人的终极证明。每位技术负责人都梦想有这样一支团队：大家乐于共事、对所构建之物充满干劲、运转得像一台上了油的机器。一支被公认为可靠、高效、能持续交付影响力的团队。

— PDF p.197 —

But it's also one of the hardest things to achieve.

但这也是最难实现的成就之一。

Most teams don't struggle because they lack talent or tools. They struggle because they have the wrong idea of what a high-performing team actually is, and more importantly, what behaviors, principles, and habits are needed to build one. That's why in this section, I want to break some of the most common myths around high-performing teams and instead give you a clear, practical view of what “high-performing” really means and how to get there.

大多数团队之所以挣扎，并非因为缺少人才或工具。它们挣扎，是因为对“什么是高绩效团队”存在错误的理解，更重要的是，对“需要哪些行为、原则和习惯才能建成它”存在误解。因此在本节里，我想打破围绕高绩效团队的一些最常见迷思，转而给你一个清晰、务实的视角：究竟什么叫“高绩效”，以及如何抵达那里。

I'll start by redefining what a high-performing team truly looks like, beyond just fast delivery or coding velocity. Then, I'll walk you through the five key dynamics that make these teams successful, how to build and protect a healthy team culture, how to create and maintain psychological safety, and finally, how to evaluate if your team is actually high-performing.

我会先重新定义高绩效团队究竟是什么样子——超越单纯的快速交付或编码速度。然后，我会带你了解让这些团队成功的五大关键动力、如何建立并守护健康的团队文化、如何创造并维持心理安全感，最后，如何评估你的团队是否真的高绩效。

High performance goes beyond output; it's shaped by how your team works, thinks, collaborates, and grows. As a tech lead, you play a critical role in enabling that growth.

高绩效超越产出本身；它由团队如何工作、如何思考、如何协作、如何成长所塑造。作为技术负责人，你在促成这种成长中扮演着关键角色。

Understand the Five Dynamics of a High-Performing Team理解高绩效团队的五大动力

Google conducted one of the most well-known studies on effective software engineering teams, known as Project Aristotle. Starting in 2012, Google spent two years studying 180 teams, 115 in engineering and 65 in sales, examining over 250 different team attributes. The goal was to identify what makes some teams more successful than others. Instead of focusing on individual talent, the study found that how team members interact with each other is the most critical factor.

Google 做过一项关于高效软件工程团队的著名研究，名为“亚里士多德计划”（Project Aristotle）。从 2012 年起，Google 花了两年时间研究了 180 个团队——其中工程团队 115 个、销售团队 65 个——考察了超过 250 项不同的团队属性。目标是找出是什么让某些团队比其他团队更成功。研究发现：关键不在于个人天赋，而在于团队成员之间如何互动，这才是最重要的因素。

Through this research, Google identified five key dynamics that define high-performing teams: psychological safety, dependability, structure and clarity, meaning, and impact. When I first came across these, I immediately reflected on how they applied to a team I led, one that was consistently described as high-performing.

通过这项研究，Google 提炼出定义高绩效团队的五大关键动力：心理安全感、可靠性、结构与清晰性、意义感、以及影响力。当我第一次看到这些时，立刻对照反思它们如何适用于我曾带领的一支团队——那支团队一直被认为是高绩效的。

Psychological safety心理安全感

Having psychological safety in a team means that everyone feels safe to share ideas, challenge decisions, take ownership without fear of judgment or punishment, openly express their thoughts, admit mistakes, and ask questions without hesitation.

团队拥有心理安全感，意味着每个人都能放心地分享想法、质疑决策、承担责任而不必担心被评判或惩罚、公开表达自己的想法、承认错误、以及毫不犹豫地提问。

In our team, psychological safety meant we had a culture where speaking up was encouraged, and no one was afraid to challenge the status quo. Even though we came from different backgrounds and cultures, openness was a core part of how we worked. If something was bothering someone, they spoke up, whether it was about blockers, frustrations, or disagreements. They were vocal with me, with the team, and even with the client.

在我们团队里，心理安全感意味着我们有一种鼓励发声的文化，没有人害怕挑战现状。尽管我们来自不同的背景和文化，开放却是我们工作方式的核心。如果有人心里有事，他们就会说出来——无论是阻塞、挫败，还是分歧。他们会对我直言、对团队直言，甚至对客户直言。

— PDF p.198 —

People asked “Why?,” “Why like this?,” “Why now?” constantly. Overcommunication became one of our most annoying and effective habits. We repeated things as many times as needed, reinforcing ideas and clarifying misunderstandings. There was no “You should already know this” or “Why are you asking this now?”

人们不停地问“为什么？”“为什么是这样？”“为什么是现在？”过度沟通成了我们最烦人、却也最有效的习惯之一。我们会按需反复讲同一件事，强化共识、澄清误解。这里没有“你早该知道这个”，也没有“你怎么现在才问”。

This openness extended beyond our team. Because we were so transparent, our stakeholders became more open and direct with us. Instead of vague conversations full of political correctness, discussions were clear and straightforward. We would hear things like “We need to go to market fast with this feature. We will pay the price of tech debt in the next iteration,” and they actually followed through when we later said, “This time we need to do it right.”

这种开放还延伸到了团队之外。因为我们如此透明，干系人对我们也变得更开放、更直接。讨论不再是满是政治正确的含糊对话，而是清晰、坦率。我们会听到这样的话：“这个功能我们得快速上市，技术债的代价我们下一轮迭代再还。”而当我们后来说“这一次我们要把它做对”时，他们也确实照做了。

You can find more on this in the section “How to Create Psychological Safety on Your Team” on page 188.

关于这一点，可参见第 188 页“如何在团队中建立心理安全感”一节。

Dependability可靠性

A high-performing team is reliable: things get done, up to the standard of quality, on time, consistently. This was one of the key pieces of feedback I kept getting from our stakeholders: “I can rely on you. I know things will either be delivered on time or I will know about any blockers or possible issues way ahead of time. I don't have to worry.”

高绩效团队是可靠的：事情能被完成，质量达标、按时交付、始终如一。这是我从干系人那里反复听到的一条关键反馈：“我可以信赖你们。我知道事情要么按时交付，要么任何阻塞或潜在问题我都会提前很久就知道。我不必担心。”

We were consistently delivering value, and this came from always challenging the value of the work we were doing and constantly asking the why behind it. Stakeholders knew that if we committed to something, it would either be delivered on time or they would be informed well in advance of any issues.

我们持续交付价值，而这来自始终对所做工作的价值提出质疑、不断追问背后的“为什么”。干系人知道，只要我们承诺了某件事，它要么按时交付，要么任何问题都会提前很久告知他们。

People would take initiative. When a blocker or a problem arose, they would reach out to other teams, talk to stakeholders, reach out to the whole company, making use of #general channels, just to get the thing done. Getting approval before acting was not our way. We were more of an “ask for forgiveness instead of permission” group. While this tendency tended to provoke my anxiety, as sometimes I felt like I was losing track of all the moving pieces, overall, their proactiveness and autonomy benefited me greatly; I never felt like a bottleneck in their way.

人们会主动采取行动。当出现阻塞或问题时，他们会主动联系其他团队、找干系人沟通、动用 #general 频道联系全公司，只为把事情办成。行动前先请示不是我们的风格。我们更像一个“请求宽恕而非请求许可”的群体。虽然这种倾向有时会让我焦虑——因为有时我感觉自己快跟不上所有这些动态了——但总体而言，他们的主动性和自治让我受益匪浅；我从没觉得自己成了挡路的瓶颈。

That reliability was fully embedded in how we operated internally. We could rely on each other as a group: we made sure no one was ever blocked for long. We used pair programming, knowledge-sharing sessions, and daily tech huddles to prevent knowledge silos. Standups weren't just status updates; they were about identifying blockers and helping each other move forward. We often said things like “It'd be good if another pair took a look at this; we've been stuck for three days and need a fresh perspective.”

这种可靠性完全融入了我们内部的运作方式。作为一个群体，我们可以彼此信赖：我们确保没有人会长时间被阻塞。我们用结对编程、知识分享会和每日技术碰头来防止知识孤岛。站会不只是状态同步，更是为了识别阻塞、互相帮助往前走。我们常说这样的话：“要是有另一对人来看一下这个就好了；我们已经卡了三天，需要点新鲜视角。”

— PDF p.199 —

We extended that same mindset beyond the team. We kept dedicated Slack channels open with the teams who relied on us and made sure communication stayed consistent and smooth. We were always available to support others, and team members regularly jumped into conversations in other parts of the company when they had something valuable to add.

我们把同样的心态延伸到团队之外。我们与依赖我们的团队保持专门的 Slack 频道畅通，确保沟通持续、顺畅。我们随时愿意支持他人；当团队成员在公司其他部门的对话中有有价值的东西可补充时，也会经常主动加入。

Even in a remote setup, we prioritized real-time conversations; for example, we preferred a quick call over a long Slack thread. Not everyone agrees with that approach, but I found that it created a sense of presence and dependability. People knew we were there, ready to talk things through. Of course, for this to work well, the calls had to be focused: we clarified the problem and outlined the key questions in advance to respect everyone's time. Whatever we discussed and clarified on the call was then shared back in the Slack thread so everyone stayed in the loop.

即便在远程模式下，我们也优先选择实时对话；例如，我们宁愿打个快速电话，也不愿扯一长串 Slack 消息。并非所有人都认同这种做法，但我发现它营造出一种“在场感”和可靠感。人们知道我们就在那里，准备好把问题谈清楚。当然，要让这招奏效，通话必须聚焦：我们会提前澄清问题、列好关键疑问，以尊重每个人的时间。通话中讨论和澄清的内容，随后会回到 Slack 线程里同步，让所有人都在信息圈里。

Structure and clarity结构与清晰性

While adaptability was key, we also had well-defined processes to provide stability and clarity. Flexibility allowed us to respond to change, but structure ensured we weren't reinventing the wheel every time. Everything had a clear structure: delivery, deployment, onboarding, decision making, progress tracking, goals, ways of working, growth, and roles definition.

虽然适应性是关键，我们也有界定清晰的流程来提供稳定和明确。灵活性让我们能应对变化，而结构确保我们不必每次都重造轮子。每件事都有清晰的结构：交付、部署、入职、决策、进展跟踪、目标、工作方式、成长、以及角色定义。

I am a huge fan of documentation, so I constantly encouraged my team to track changes on architecture diagrams, retro discussions, infrastructure changes (tracked through an infrastructure-as-code process), and decisions. This made onboarding a breeze, ensuring new team members quickly understood how we worked and their role in it. It also kept our day-to-day running smoothly; everyone knew exactly what was expected of them and what to focus on, which enabled efficiency and speed.

我特别推崇文档，因此不断鼓励团队把变更记录在架构图、复盘讨论、基础设施改动（通过基础设施即代码流程跟踪）以及各项决策中。这让入职变得轻而易举，确保新成员迅速理解我们如何工作、以及自己在其中的角色。它也让我们的日常运转顺畅；每个人都清楚对自己的期望是什么、该聚焦什么，从而带来效率和速度。

Meaning and impact意义感与影响力

I grouped these two concepts together because they overlap: they both refer to the extent to which team members feel their work has a purpose and is making a difference, whether in the organization or society. We all want our work to be meaningful at some level, and we all know how important it is that people believe in what they do. When people feel connected to the purpose of their work, it has a massive impact on motivation and engagement. This is a game-changer for a tech team.

我把这两个概念放在一起，因为它们有重叠：二者都指团队成员在多大程度上感到自己的工作是有目的、能带来改变的——无论是在组织内还是在社会上。我们都希望自己的工作在某种层面上是有意义的；我们也都知道，人们相信自己所做之事有多么重要。当人们感到与工作的目的相连时，会对动力和投入产生巨大影响。这对一支技术团队来说是颠覆性的。

— PDF p.200 —

The mistake many companies make is involving developers too late in the process, only after the product has been defined. But in our case, our PM included us from step one, the initial brainstorming. We were part of the ideation phase, free to ask questions and challenge assumptions. This is crucial because developers are often assumed to be uninterested in the “why” behind a product, when in reality, they often don't see the value simply because they were never included in the conversation.

很多公司犯的错，是让开发者太晚介入流程——往往等产品都定义好了才叫上他们。但在我们的情形里，产品经理从第一步、从最初的头脑风暴就把我们拉了进来。我们参与了构思阶段，可以自由提问、挑战假设。这一点至关重要，因为人们常常以为开发者对产品背后的“为什么”不感兴趣；而实际上，他们之所以看不到价值，往往只是因为从未被纳入那场对话。

Being involved from the start has two key benefits. First, the whole team gains a deep understanding of why they are building something, who it helps, what problem it solves, and why it matters. This alignment ensures that every decision and line of code contributes meaningfully to the final product. Second, team members see a clear connection between their daily tasks and the bigger picture, making even routine work feel impactful.

从一开始就参与有两个关键好处。第一，整个团队会深刻理解自己为什么构建某个东西、它帮助谁、解决什么问题、以及为什么重要。这种对齐确保每一个决策、每一行代码都对最终产品有意义地做出贡献。第二，团队成员能看清日常任务与大局之间的清晰联系，让哪怕是例行工作也显得有影响力。

Another common mistake is assuming that meaningful work applies only to customer-facing features, revenue-generating initiatives, or socially impactful projects. But different people find meaning in different things. In our case, we worked on maintaining and migrating a huge monolith. Even though it was the “money-maker” product of our client, it was still something that could feel tedious for developers. What motivated us wasn't its impact on revenue but the technical challenge of understanding this massive system, improving its quality, and migrating it without breaking anything. It was like solving a giant puzzle.

另一个常见错误，是以为“有意义的工作”只适用于面向用户的功能、产生收入的项目、或有社会影响力的项目。但不同的人会在不同的事物中找到意义。我们当时做的是维护和迁移一个庞大的单体系统。尽管它是客户的“印钞机”产品，对开发者来说仍可能显得枯燥。真正激励我们的，不是它对收入的影响，而是理解这个巨型系统、提升其质量、并在不搞坏任何东西的前提下完成迁移所带来的技术挑战。那就像在解一个巨大的拼图。

The same applies to platform teams. Because their users are internal teams rather than customers, many struggle to connect their work to the end product. But once they spend time with the teams using their tools and see the direct impact of their work, their motivation increases significantly.

平台团队也是如此。因为他们的用户是内部团队而非外部客户，很多人难以把自己的工作与最终产品联系起来。但一旦他们花时间和使用其工具的团队待在一起、亲眼看到自己工作的直接影响，他们的动力就会显著提升。

Doing impactful work is just the first step. Equally important is making that work visible. I made it a habit to highlight my team's accomplishments and challenges in every possible setting. As a tech lead, you're often the only person from your team in the room, whether it's with clients, executives, or other stakeholders. That makes it your responsibility to represent your team effectively. Show up prepared, with a clear understanding of progress, open questions, and any blockers. Don't just report status; advocate for your team and make their contributions visible.

做出有影响力的工作只是第一步。同样重要的是让这份工作被看见。我养成了一个习惯：在一切可能的场合凸显团队的成就与挑战。作为技术负责人，无论是面对客户、高管还是其他干系人，你往往是房间里唯一来自你团队的人。这就让“有效地代表你的团队”成了你的责任。到场前要做好准备，清楚掌握进展、悬而未决的问题和任何阻塞。不要只汇报状态；要为你的团队发声，让他们的贡献被看见。

I encouraged my team to use every opportunity to make our work visible, starting with showcases. One of the most effective examples was our quarterly client showcase. While many teams treated it as a checkbox exercise, throwing together slides an hour before, I saw it as a powerful platform to highlight our impact, especially to stakeholders and teams we didn't interact with day to day.

我鼓励团队利用一切机会让我们的工作被看见，展示会（showcase）就是其中之一。最有效的例子之一是我们每季度一次的客户展示会。很多团队把它当成一项打勾了事的任务，提前一小时匆匆凑出幻灯片；而我把它看作一个凸显我们影响力的有力平台，尤其能触达那些我们日常并不打交道的干系人和团队。

— PDF p.201 —

So we treated showcases like any other deliverable. We added a dedicated preparation task to our board, prioritized it, estimated the time it would take to prepare, and planned it with clear expectations. We made sure to include context about our team, any changes since the last quarter, a rundown of accomplishments both big and small, the challenges we faced, and what was coming next. Everyone on the team was involved, and we ran dry runs to stay within the time limit and polish the delivery.

因此我们像对待任何其他交付物一样对待展示会。我们在看板上加了一个专门的准备任务，给它排优先级、估算准备所需时间，并带着清晰的预期去规划。我们确保内容包括：团队背景、上个季度以来的变化、大大小小成就的盘点、我们面临的挑战、以及接下来的计划。团队每个人都参与进来，我们还做了彩排，以控制时长、打磨呈现效果。

These sessions weren't just about recognition, though the positive feedback we received was motivating. They became moments of reflection and celebration, a chance for the team to step back and appreciate what we had achieved together. Over time, they also became a valuable way for team members to develop their presentation and storytelling skills, which helped build confidence and visibility across the organization.

这些分享会不只是为了获得认可——尽管收到的正面反馈确实很鼓舞人。它们成了反思和庆祝的时刻，让团队有机会退后一步，共同欣赏我们一起取得的成就。久而久之，它们也成了团队成员锻炼表达与讲故事能力的宝贵途径，有助于在整个组织内建立信心和能见度。

This doesn't mean we were perfect; no team is. Every time you solve one problem, another appears. Overcommunication can be frustrating. Constantly challenging each other could get exhausting. And as a tech lead, you never feel like things are truly “smooth,” because if you're focused on improvement, there's always something to work on. The key is keeping the bigger picture in mind, questioning why you're doing things the way you are, and being open to evolving your ways of working. What made us efficient was our honesty, our ability to talk things through, and our willingness to adapt, even when challenges came up.

这并不意味着我们完美；没有哪个团队是完美的。每当你解决一个问题，另一个又会冒出来。过度沟通可能令人烦躁，不断互相挑战也可能让人疲惫。而作为技术负责人，你永远不会觉得事情真正“顺了”，因为只要你专注于改进，就总有可做的事。关键是牢记大局、追问自己为什么照现在这样做事、并乐于演进工作方式。让我们高效的，是我们的坦诚、把问题谈透的能力，以及即便挑战来临也愿意适应的态度。

In conclusion, a high-performing team is not defined by having the best developers, making no mistakes, or always meeting deadlines, and it's definitely not about being perfect. Instead, it's a group of people who care about each other, work well together, and have a healthy team culture, as the team results are deeply tied to how people collaborate, not just individual skills.

总而言之，一支高绩效团队，并不以拥有最强的开发者、从不犯错、或总能按期交付来定义，更绝不是追求完美。相反，它是一群互相关心、协作融洽、拥有健康团队文化的人；因为团队的成果深深取决于人们如何协作，而不仅仅是个人技能。

How to Build a Healthy Team Culture如何打造健康的团队文化

Team culture is how you work together, shaped by shared values, behaviors, and team norms. It's intangible and hard to measure, but it influences everything: how decisions get made, how fast you move, how people communicate, and how feedback flows.

团队文化就是你们共同工作的方式，由共享的价值观、行为和团队规范塑造。它无形、难以衡量，却影响着一切：决策如何做出、行动有多快、人们如何沟通、反馈如何流动。

While you can't track culture with a single metric, there are clear signs when something is off. In teams with a weak culture, trust is often missing. People hesitate to speak up, avoid risks, and hold back feedback. Collaboration drops.

虽然你无法用单一指标来跟踪文化，但当出问题时会有明显迹象。在文化薄弱的团队里，信任往往缺失。人们怯于发声、回避风险、吝啬反馈。协作减少。

— PDF p.202 —

Problems get pointed out, but no one steps in to solve them. Decision making slows, and progress grinds down.

问题被指出来了，却没有人站出来解决。决策变慢，进展也逐渐停滞。

In contrast, a strong culture feels energized. People feel safe, take ownership, offer feedback freely, and support each other. They challenge ideas without fear and focus on making things better.

相比之下，强大的文化让人感到充满活力。人们感到安全、主动担责、自由地给予反馈、彼此支持。他们毫无畏惧地挑战想法，并专注于把事情做得更好。

Whether you like it or not, every team has a culture. The question is whether you're shaping it intentionally or letting it form by accident. If your team's dynamics don't reflect your values or expectations, the most effective way to change that is to shape the culture from day one.

无论你喜不喜欢，每个团队都有一种文化。问题在于：你是在有意识地塑造它，还是任由它偶然形成。如果你团队的氛围并不反映你的价值观或期望，最有效的改变方式，就是从第一天起就主动塑造文化。

One of the most powerful ways to do that is by aligning on how you'll work together. Every time a new person joins, the team changes. Don't assume everyone shares the same expectations. Instead, make them explicit.

其中最有力的方式之一，就是就“你们将如何协作”达成一致。每有新人加入，团队就变了。不要假设大家都抱有同样的期望。相反，把期望明确地讲出来。

A simple and powerful tool is a “Ways of Working” session. This is a structured conversation you run when forming a new team or when major changes happen. The goal is to agree on how the team will operate. This can include how feedback is given, how decisions are made, how often you run retrospectives, and anything else that shapes the team experience.

一个简单而有力的工具，是一场“工作方式”讨论会。这是在组建新团队、或发生重大变化时开展的一次结构化对话。目标是就团队将如何运作达成一致。内容可以包括：如何给予反馈、如何做决策、多久开一次复盘、以及其他一切会塑造团队体验的事情。

— PDF p.203 —

The intention of the session is surfacing assumptions. Write them down, talk through them, and listen for disagreement. You'll often uncover mismatches you didn't expect. That's where the value is. For example, one person might expect pull requests to be reviewed within a few hours, while another thinks 48 hours is totally reasonable. Or you might have different understandings of what “done” means; does it mean merged or fully deployed to production? Clarifying those early prevents future misalignment and gives you a shared foundation to return to.

这场讨论的目的，是把各种假设摆到台面上。把它们写下来、逐一讨论，并留意分歧。你常常会发现一些意料之外的错位。价值正在于此。例如，有人可能期望 pull request 在几小时内被 review，而另一个人觉得 48 小时完全合理。又或者你们对“完成”的理解不同：它是指合并，还是指完整部署到生产？尽早澄清这些，能防止日后的错位，并给你一个可以反复回归的共同基础。

Teams aren't static, so team processes shouldn't be either. Every time someone joins or leaves, you have a new team. Dynamics, needs, and expectations shift. What worked before might need rethinking. For example, when a new team member joined, we realized our 9 AM standup clashed with their child's school drop-off routine. We discussed it together and moved it to 10 AM. Small adjustments like this can go a long way in supporting inclusion, morale, and team performance.

团队不是静止的，团队流程也不应静止。每有人加入或离开，你就有了一个新团队。氛围、需求和期望都会变化。过去管用的做法可能需要重新思考。例如，当一位新成员加入时，我们发现早上 9 点的站会与他送孩子上学的时间冲突。我们一起商量后把它改到了 10 点。这样的小调整，对支持包容、士气和团队绩效大有帮助。

This document becomes an anchor. When things drift, feedback sessions stop happening, or decisions start getting made in silos, you can return to what you agreed on and ask the team, “Do we want to change this? Or recommit to it?”

这份文档会成为一个锚点。当事情跑偏、反馈环节停摆、或决策开始在孤岛里做出来时，你可以回到当初商定的内容，问团队：“我们是想改一改？还是重新承诺坚守它？”

It also becomes a powerful onboarding tool. Instead of new hires guessing how the team works or making assumptions, they can see the team's expectations clearly from day one. It helps them integrate faster and more confidently.

它还会成为一个有力的入职工具。新人不必去猜团队怎么运作、或凭空假设，而是从第一天起就能清楚看到团队的期望。这帮他们更快、更自信地融入。

You can even use this shared agreement in hiring. It gives candidates a clear sense of what it's like to work on the team and helps you assess fit more meaningfully.

你甚至可以在招聘中使用这份共同约定。它让候选人清楚地感受到在这个团队工作是什么样，也帮你更有意义地评估契合度。

As you define and evolve how your team works, it's critical to make sure those processes are actually working for everyone, not just the loudest voices or the most experienced members. Inclusion doesn't happen automatically. It has to be built into the way you run meetings, gather feedback, and make decisions. Every process you design, like retrospectives, standups, one-on-ones, should be intentionally inclusive. For example, when running retrospectives, use multiple ways to gather input: out loud, Post-its, anonymous forms. People have different communication styles, and a one-size-fits-all approach limits participation.

在定义并演进团队工作方式时，至关重要的是确保这些流程真正对每个人都奏效，而不只是对声音最大或最资深的成员。包容不会自动发生。它必须被嵌入你开会、收集反馈、做决策的方式里。你设计的每一个流程——复盘、站会、一对一面谈——都应是刻意包容的。例如，开复盘时，用多种方式收集意见：口头表达、便利贴、匿名表单。人们有不同的沟通风格，一刀切的做法会限制参与。

Here are some key processes every team should define and continuously revisit:

以下是每个团队都应定义、并持续回顾的关键流程：

  • Onboarding — This helps new members integrate quickly and understand how the team works.入职 —— 帮新成员快速融入、理解团队如何运作。
  • Hiring (if applicable) — The team's values and ways of working should be reflected in how you assess candidates.招聘（如适用）—— 团队的价值观和工作方式应体现在你评估候选人的方式中。
  • One-on-ones between tech leads and each team member — These build trust, uncover blockers, and maintain alignment.技术负责人与每位成员的一对一面谈 —— 建立信任、发现阻塞、保持对齐。
  • Standups — Daily or regular check-ins that highlight progress, blockers, and opportunities to help.站会 —— 每日或定期的同步，凸显进展、阻塞和可以搭把手的地方。
  • Progress tracking — A system that's visible and understandable to both the team and stakeholders. Avoid tools that are too technical or go unused. If nobody's using it, revisit or remove it.进展跟踪 —— 一套团队和干系人都看得见、看得懂的系统。避免用过于技术化、或没人用的工具。如果没人用它，就重新审视或弃用。
  • Retrospectives — Structured reflection points to discuss what's working, what's not, and how to improve, generating improvement actions.复盘 —— 结构化的反思环节，讨论哪些有效、哪些无效、以及如何改进，并产出改进行动项。
— PDF p.204 —

Even if your team is small or just getting started, having these foundations in place makes a big difference. They don't need to be complicated; they just need to be intentional. Every process you define contributes to shaping a team culture where people feel safe, supported, and set up to thrive.

即便你的团队很小、或刚刚起步，把这些基础打牢也会大有不同。它们不必复杂；只需是刻意为之。你定义的每一个流程，都在共同塑造一种让人们感到安全、被支持、并能茁壮成长的团队文化。

How to Create Psychological Safety on Your Team如何在团队中建立心理安全感

The first sign of a healthy team culture is that everyone feels safe to speak up, ask questions, and take risks without fear of judgment. This kind of safety is foundational to team performance. You can't even begin to address other team issues until it's in place. But, as important as it is, creating it isn't easy. In the following sections, I'll share some ways you can build it as a tech lead.

健康团队文化的第一个信号，就是每个人都能安全地发声、提问、承担风险，而不必担心被评判。这种安全感是团队绩效的基石。在它就位之前，你甚至无法着手解决其他团队问题。但尽管它如此重要，建立它却并不容易。在接下来的小节里，我会分享一些作为技术负责人可以建立它的方法。

Act as an example以身作则

The best tool you have to shape your team's culture is yourself. If you expect people to behave a certain way, you have to consistently model that behavior. Your actions speak louder than any values slide or process document.

你用来塑造团队文化的最好工具，就是你自己。如果你期望人们以某种方式行事，你就必须始终如一地示范这种行为。你的行动，比任何价值观幻灯片或流程文件都更有说服力。

As a tech lead, you set the tone more than anyone else. How you give feedback, how open you are to criticism, how well you listen: these all send strong signals to your team. While psychological safety is a shared responsibility, your behavior sets the foundation.

作为技术负责人，你比任何人都更能定下基调。你如何给予反馈、你对批评有多开放、你倾听得有多好——这些都在向团队传递强烈信号。虽然心理安全感是共同的责任，但你的行为奠定了基础。

Your team looks to you for cues, and the way you handle mistakes, feedback, and collaboration directly shapes how safe others feel to speak up and contribute. So constantly keep yourself in check: reflect on your behavior and actions and the impact it has on your team, and adapt if needed.

你的团队会从你身上寻找信号；你处理错误、反馈和协作的方式，直接塑造了其他人敢不敢发声和贡献。因此要不断自我检视：反思你的行为与举动、及其对团队的影响，并在需要时做出调整。

Normalize failure让失败变得平常

One of the best ways to build psychological safety is to change how failure is perceived, both human failure (like making a mistake or not knowing something) and system failure (like production incidents or process breakdowns). Mistakes are inevitable in both areas. So instead of hiding them or punishing them, bring them into the open and make learning from failure part of how your team works.

建立心理安全感最好的方式之一，是改变人们对失败的看法——既包括人的失败（比如犯了错、或不知道某件事），也包括系统的失败（比如生产事故或流程崩溃）。这两方面的错误都不可避免。因此，不要隐藏它们、也不要惩罚它们，而是把它们摆到明面上，让“从失败中学习”成为团队工作方式的一部分。

Encourage your team to take ownership of their mistakes and admit when they don't know something. Support them in taking risks and using failure as a chance to learn and grow, instead of being afraid of how others might react. And the best way to teach this is by doing it yourself. Start by admitting when you don't know something. A lot of tech leads feel pressure to always have the answers, but showing your team that it's OK to say “I don't know” builds trust. If they see you do it, they'll feel safer doing the same. The next step is asking for clarification—“Can you please explain this again?—instead of staying quiet.

鼓励团队为自己的错误担责，并在不知道某件事时坦然承认。支持他们承担风险、把失败当作学习和成长的机会，而不是害怕别人会作何反应。而教这一点最好的方式，就是你自己先做。从承认自己不知道某件事开始。很多技术负责人觉得必须始终有答案，但向团队展示“说一句‘我不知道’也没关系”，恰恰能建立信任。如果他们看到你这么做，自己做时就会更安心。下一步是主动请求澄清——“你能把这个再解释一遍吗？”——而不是保持沉默。

— PDF p.205 —

Chances are, someone else in the room is feeling just as lost.

很可能，房间里还有另一个人跟你一样没搞明白。

Own your mistakes. Say, “I'm sorry, I made a mistake.” Acknowledge what happened instead of pretending it didn't. Start small: share when you mixed up a date or used the wrong variable. As that becomes more natural, you'll get more comfortable being open about bigger issues too. This creates space for others to do the same.

为自己的错误担责。说一句：“对不起，我搞错了。”承认发生了什么，而不是假装它没发生。从小处做起：搞混了日期、用错了变量，就说出来。当这变得越来越自然，你也会更自在地公开更大的问题。这会为其他人创造同样去做的空间。

Failure is one of the best opportunities for growth because we tend to stop and reflect only when things go wrong. For example, in one of my teams, a release unexpectedly took down a key part of the product. It was stressful at the moment, but the team came together afterward to run a postmortem. That session led to some of our best process improvements, from better automated tests to tighter release checklists, that we might not have prioritized otherwise.

失败是成长最好的机会之一，因为我们往往只有在出问题时才会停下来反思。例如，在我的一个团队里，一次发布意外搞挂了产品的一个关键部分。当时压力很大，但事后团队聚在一起做了复盘。那次复盘带来了我们一些最好的流程改进——从更好的自动化测试到更严密的发布检查清单——这些改进换作平时我们可能不会优先去做。

Postmortems are a great tool for learning, but they work only if you run them with the right mindset. Instead of trying to find someone to blame, focus on what went wrong. What failed in the process? What were the conditions that led to the mistake? And how can we prevent it from happening again? The goal is to make sure it doesn't happen again, no matter who's involved.

复盘是学习的好工具，但只有带着正确的心态去开才管用。不要试图去找该怪谁，而要聚焦于哪里出了问题。流程中哪一环失败了？是哪些条件导致了这个错误？我们又该如何防止它再次发生？目标是确保它不再发生，无论涉及谁。

Let's say someone broke production with a commit, and it took ages to revert because your deployment pipeline is slow. Instead of pointing fingers, use that moment to ask: how can we make this better for everyone? Maybe the pipeline needs to be faster. Maybe you need to add feature flags so you can turn things off quickly when something goes wrong. The point is to make recovery easier, reduce pressure on individuals, and improve the system, not to blame someone for triggering the problem.

假设有人一次提交搞挂了生产环境，而因为部署流水线很慢，回滚花了很久。不要指责任何人，而是借这个机会问：我们怎样才能让这件事对所有人都更容易？也许流水线需要更快。也许你需要加上 feature flag，以便出问题时能迅速关掉。重点是让恢复更容易、减轻个人压力、改进系统，而不是因为有人触发了问题就去怪他。

Another great way to normalize failure is by creating a controlled environment where experimentation is encouraged and mistakes are easy to recover from. For example, having a strong set of automated tests, an integrated development environment, smooth rollback processes, and well-defined staging workflows that mirror production allows people to take action without the fear of irreversible damage.

让失败常态化的另一个好办法，是创造一个受控环境：在其中鼓励实验，并且犯错后容易恢复。例如，拥有一套完善的自动化测试、一体化的开发环境、顺畅的回滚流程，以及一套与生产镜像的、定义清晰的预发布工作流，就能让人们放心行动，而不必害怕造成不可逆的损害。

Some teams even run “game days,” structured exercises where a team member intentionally injects a fault into the system and the rest of the team conducts a mock incident response.

有些团队甚至会搞“游戏日”（game day）：一种结构化演练，由某位成员故意向系统注入一个故障，其余人则进行一次模拟的事故响应。

In one of my teams, we used a tool called Chaos Monkey, which was designed to randomly shut down services in our production environment. While it sounds risky, we used it carefully and intentionally to test the resilience of our systems and processes. It forced us to build more fault-tolerant architecture and improved our team's confidence in handling unexpected failures. You don't need to go this far to benefit from the same mindset. But aiming for this level of trust in your systems, where failure can be tested safely, is a goal worth working toward.

在我的一个团队里，我们用过一个叫 Chaos Monkey 的工具，它的设计就是随机关停生产环境中的服务。听起来很冒险，但我们谨慎而有意识地用它来测试系统和流程的韧性。它迫使我们构建更容错的架构，并提升了团队应对意外故障的信心。你不必做到这么极端，也能从同样的心态中受益。但把“对系统达到这种程度的信任、可以安全地测试失败”作为努力目标，是值得的。

— PDF p.206 —

In a team where failure is normalized, people feel safer to experiment, speak up, and take initiative. That's how you build a team that learns fast, improves constantly, and supports each other through the ups and downs of product development.

在一个让失败常态化的团队里，人们会更安全地去实验、发声和主动行动。这就是你打造一支学得快、持续改进、并在产品开发的起伏中互相扶持的团队的方式。

Plan for failure, not just success为失败做计划，而不只计划成功

I remember this time my team was doing a huge migration from one system to another. Everything seemed ready, but I had a gut feeling something was off, something that stopped me from pulling the switch. I tried explaining my worry to the team, and we double-checked everything, but I still couldn't put my finger on what exactly was wrong. So instead of endlessly checking again, we came up with a different approach: preparing for failure as much as for success. We shifted our thinking from “How do we avoid something happening?” to a set of questions like “What if it goes wrong?,” “Who will fix it?,” “Can we roll back the change?” We made a plan: who would be on call if things went wrong overnight, who needed to be informed about the problem, what the financial impact could be. We even flagged it to our PM: “Something might go wrong, but we're ready to handle it.”

我记得有一次，我的团队在做一次从一个系统到另一个系统的大型迁移。一切看起来都准备好了，但我直觉感到哪里不对劲——正是这种感觉让我没敢按下开关。我试着把担忧讲给团队听，我们又把所有东西复核了一遍，但我仍然说不清到底哪里不对。于是，与其无休止地反复检查，我们换了个做法：像为成功做准备一样为失败做准备。我们把思路从“我们如何避免出事？”转变成一组问题：“如果出问题怎么办？”“谁来修？”“我们能回滚这次变更吗？”我们制定了计划：如果夜里出问题谁来 on call、需要通知谁、可能造成多大的财务影响。我们甚至向产品经理打了预防针：“可能会出点状况，但我们已经准备好应对。”

Unfortunately, my hunch was right. Errors started rolling in during the night. It took us a while to fix them, but we were ready. We had a plan. And honestly, looking back, moments like that were great team-building exercises. Everyone was focused on solving a common problem, everyone was equally part of the decision, and it didn't matter who wrote the commit; it mattered that we agreed together to go for it.

不幸的是，我的直觉是对的。夜里错误开始涌进来。我们花了一些时间才修好，但我们早有准备。我们有计划。说实话，回头看，那样的时刻是绝佳的团队建设。每个人都专注于解决同一个问题，每个人都平等地参与了决策；谁写的提交并不重要，重要的是我们共同决定去做这件事。

It was also a great learning opportunity. We grew from it. We got better not just at shipping code but at thinking ahead, at supporting each other under pressure, and at owning the outcome together.

那也是一次极好的学习机会。我们从中成长。我们不仅在发布代码上，更在提前预判、在压力下互相支持、以及共同承担结果方面变得更强。

Also, by describing the worst-case scenario and having a clear plan to deal with it, you make people less afraid, because the biggest fear is often fear of the unknown.

此外，通过把最坏情况描述出来、并制定清晰的应对计划，你会让人们不那么害怕，因为最大的恐惧往往是对未知的恐惧。

How you deal with failure builds your character as a leader and shapes your team culture. So learning how to use it right benefits everyone.

你如何应对失败，塑造着你作为领导者的品格，也塑造着你的团队文化。因此学会正确地运用它，会让所有人受益。

— PDF p.207 —

Encourage honest feedback鼓励坦诚的反馈

Make feedback a key part of your team culture. It shouldn't be something you save for performance reviews; it should be part of how you work every day. When feedback becomes normal, people get used to sharing what's on their mind, what bothers them, and what could be better. It helps build a habit of honesty.

让反馈成为团队文化的关键组成部分。它不应是你攒到绩效评估时才拿出来的东西；它应是你日常工作方式的一部分。当反馈变得平常，人们就会习惯分享心里的想法、什么困扰着他们、以及哪里可以更好。这有助于养成坦诚的习惯。

You can also encourage people to use feedback in their day-to-day interactions. When someone asks you how they can grow, don't just give them your input; point them to others who work closely with them and suggest they ask for feedback there too. Or, when someone comes to you with an issue they're having with a team member, instead of jumping in to solve it for them, ask if they've shared that feedback directly. More often than not, that conversation is exactly what's needed to move forward.

你还可以鼓励人们在日常互动中运用反馈。当有人问你该如何成长时，不要只给你自己的看法；把他们引荐给与其紧密协作的其他人，建议他们也去那里征求反馈。或者，当有人带着他与某位团队成员之间的问题来找你时，不要一头扎进去替他解决，而是问问他是否已经直接向对方反馈过。很多时候，那场对话正是推动事情往前走所需要的。

The more your team gets used to sharing feedback in real time, the more comfortable they'll be being honest with each other, and with you.

你的团队越习惯实时分享反馈，他们彼此之间、以及对你，就越能坦诚相待。

More on this in Chapter 5.

这一点在第 5 章中有更多论述。

Encourage diverse perspectives鼓励多元视角

In a psychologically safe team, all perspectives are welcomed—not just tolerated but actively encouraged. As a tech lead, this means your team's day-to-day processes need to be designed with inclusion in mind. From onboarding to delivery rituals to performance reviews, every part of how your team operates should support a wide range of people, not just those who already “get how things work.”

在一个有心理安全感的团队里，所有视角都受到欢迎——不只是被容忍，而是被积极鼓励。作为技术负责人，这意味着团队的日常流程需要在设计时就把包容考虑在内。从入职到交付仪式、再到绩效评估，团队运作的每一个环节都应支持各种各样的人，而不只是那些早已“懂得这里规矩”的人。

The best teams work because their differences strengthen them. When people bring different strengths, backgrounds, and perspectives, those differences can fill gaps and elevate the whole team. As a tech lead, your role is to create the kind of environment where that can happen: where differences are valued and used well.

最优秀的团队之所以行，是因为他们的差异让他们更强。当人们带来不同的长处、背景和视角时，这些差异可以填补缺口、提升整个团队。作为技术负责人，你的角色是创造一种能让这一切发生的环境：让差异被珍视、被善用。

This starts by asking the team how they work best. Get a sense of how each person prefers to receive feedback, what makes them feel comfortable sharing ideas, and how they like to make decisions together. These conversations might feel small, but they shape whether people feel heard, or invisible.

这从询问团队“你们怎样工作最好”开始。了解每个人更喜欢如何接收反馈、什么让他们安心分享想法、以及他们喜欢怎样共同做决策。这些对话看似很小，但它们决定了人们是感到被倾听、还是被无视。

The onboarding experience is one of the earliest and clearest signals of whether a team truly supports diverse perspectives. Without a good onboarding process, the people most likely to thrive are those who've worked at similar companies before. Everyone else, especially those coming from different industries, backgrounds, or cultures, starts at a disadvantage. For example, without high-quality onboarding, engineers joining a fast-moving tech company from a non-digital-first company might struggle to find their footing in the first months and be more likely to leave.

入职体验是一个团队是否真正支持多元视角的最早、也最清晰的信号之一。没有好的入职流程，最可能如鱼得水的，是那些曾在类似公司待过的人。其他所有人，尤其是来自不同行业、背景或文化的人，一开始就处于劣势。例如，如果没有高质量的入职，从非数字化优先的公司加入一家快速发展的科技公司的工程师，可能头几个月都难以站稳脚跟，并更有可能离职。

— PDF p.208 —

Building a psychologically safe team also means creating space for all kinds of ideas, including the strange or unconventional ones. On my team, we used to hold brainstorm sessions where the only rule was that nothing was off-limits. Anyone could propose anything, no matter how wild it sounded. And that's exactly where some of our best ideas came from: the simple, elegant solutions that we wouldn't have considered in a more constrained or judgmental environment.

打造有心理安全感的团队，还意味着为各种想法创造空间，包括那些奇怪或非传统的想法。在我的团队里，我们曾搞过头脑风暴会，唯一的规则就是“没有什么是禁区”。任何人都可以提出任何想法，不管听起来多离谱。而我们一些最好的想法恰恰就来自那里：那些简单而优雅的解决方案，若是在一个更拘束、更爱评判的环境里，我们根本不会考虑。

Of course, welcoming diverse perspectives also means learning to handle conflict. And while it might feel counterintuitive, conflict is actually a good sign. It means people care. It means they're comfortable enough to challenge each other and raise concerns. When everyone always agrees or, worse, no one speaks up at all, that's when you should worry. Healthy teams debate. They wrestle with decisions. And they emerge stronger because of it.

当然，欢迎多元视角也意味着学会处理冲突。虽然听起来反直觉，但冲突其实是个好迹象。它意味着人们在乎。意味着他们足够自在，敢于互相质疑、提出顾虑。当所有人总是一致同意、或更糟——根本没人说话时，那才是你该担心的时候。健康的团队会辩论。他们会为决策绞尽脑汁。并因此变得更强。

Inclusive collaboration also extends to technical practices like estimation. Too often, estimates are made solely by the most senior engineers on the team. But complexity isn't one-size-fits-all; what feels simple to a senior might be far more time-consuming for someone with less experience. If the task ends up in the hands of a junior engineer, will the original estimate still hold?
