Involving the whole team in estimation discussions helps surface these differences early, promotes learning, and results in more accurate, realistic plans. When you make space for open conversation around complexity, everyone's perspective has value.

包容的协作还延伸到估算等技术实践中。太多时候，估算只由团队里最资深的工程师来做。但复杂性并非一刀切：对资深者来说简单的事，对经验较浅的人可能要花多得多的时间。如果这个任务最后落到了一位初级工程师手里，当初的估算还作数吗？让整个团队参与估算讨论，有助于尽早暴露这些差异、促进学习，并带来更准确、更现实的计划。当你为围绕复杂性的开放对话留出空间时，每个人的视角都有价值。

Overcommunicate过度沟通

Overcommunication was one of my high-performing team's most effective, and occasionally most annoying, habits. We repeated things constantly: goals, updates, questions, and answers. There was no “You should know this already” or “Why are you asking this now?” We'd rather explain something one more time than risk confusion or silent struggles. Everyone was vocal: to me, to each other, and to the client.

过度沟通是我那支高绩效团队最有效、偶尔也最烦人的习惯之一。我们不停地重复各种事情：目标、进展、问题、答案。没有“你早该知道这个”，也没有“你怎么现在才问？”我们宁愿多解释一遍，也不愿冒困惑或默默挣扎的风险。每个人都直言不讳：对我、对彼此、对客户。

This openness brought many benefits but sometimes required some fine-tuning. I remember needing to have a few conversations with team members about adjusting how they communicated in front of clients. Not to silence them but to help them consider the delivery. New clients, especially, weren't always used to such direct communication. Still, the habit of overcommunicating, from asking “Why?,” “Why like this?,” “Why now?” to revisiting our goals or decisions, helped us avoid misunderstandings and supported clarity throughout our work. Even with these risks, I still believe the benefits of overcommunication outweigh the downsides, so I absolutely recommend it.

这种开放带来了很多好处，但有时也需要一些微调。我记得曾和团队成员谈过几次，请他们调整在客户面前沟通的方式。不是要让他们闭嘴，而是帮他们考虑表达方式。尤其是新客户，并不总是习惯如此直接的沟通。尽管如此，过度沟通的习惯——从追问“为什么？”“为什么这样？”“为什么现在？”，到反复重温我们的目标或决策——帮我们避免了误解，并让我们的工作始终保持清晰。即便有这些风险，我仍然相信过度沟通的利大于弊，因此我绝对推荐它。

— PDF p.209 —

Build trust建立信任

None of the strategies mentioned before can be achieved without trust in the team.

前面提到的所有策略，离开团队中的信任都无法实现。

Trust is built through constant communication, transparency, and follow-through.

信任是通过持续的沟通、透明和说到做到建立起来的。

Constant communication means having recurring checkpoints with your team through one-on-ones, or team alignment meetings like standups or plannings, and continuously sharing information and knowledge with them.

持续沟通，意味着通过一对一面谈、或站会/规划会等团队对齐会议，与团队建立周期性的检查点，并持续与他们分享信息和知识。

Transparency means being honest about blockers and possible issues, admitting to mistakes and when you don't know, and providing balanced feedback: both positive and improvement feedback.

透明，意味着坦诚面对阻塞和潜在问题、承认错误和自己不知道的时候、并给出平衡的反馈：既包括正面反馈，也包括改进建议。

Whatever you say or agree to doesn't mean much if you don't act on it. Actually, one of the simplest ways to build trust is this: say you'll do something, and then do it.

无论你说什么、答应什么，如果你不付诸行动，都没什么意义。其实，建立信任最简单的方法之一就是：说到做到。

More strategies on building and maintaining trust with your team can be found in the section “How to Build Strong Relationships” on page 62.

关于如何与团队建立并维持信任，更多策略见第 62 页“如何建立牢固关系”一节。

Psychological safety must be inclusive. If even one person doesn't feel safe, the team as a whole isn't truly safe. It counts only when everyone feels free to speak up without fear of being judged, ignored, or penalized.

心理安全感必须是包容的。哪怕只有一个人感到不安全，整个团队就不算真正安全。只有当每个人都能自由发声、而不害怕被评判、被忽视或被惩罚时，它才算数。

To understand how your team is really feeling, build regular check-ins into your team's rhythm. Retrospectives are a natural opportunity for this. Try starting with a quick safety check: ask each person to rate, on a scale from one to five, how comfortable they feel speaking up in the team. If several people respond with low numbers, that's a clear signal that psychological safety is lacking, which means the retrospective might surface the views of only the most vocal team members. In that case, pause and make psychological safety the main topic of discussion.

要了解团队真实的感受，就在团队的节奏里建立定期的检查。复盘就是一个天然的机会。可以试着从一个快速的安全感检查开始：请每个人在一到五分之间，给自己在团队里发言的自在程度打分。如果有好几个人打了低分，那就是一个清晰信号——心理安全感不足，意味着复盘可能只会暴露出最爱发声的那几个成员的观点。这种情况下，就暂停一下，把心理安全感受为主要讨论话题。

One-on-ones are another key tool. Use them not just to talk about work but to create space for people to share how they're really feeling. If you notice someone regularly holding back, withdrawing, or not contributing in meetings, bring it up gently and supportively. These conversations show that you care and that you're paying attention to more than just output; they help people feel seen and heard.

一对一面谈是另一个关键工具。不要只用它来谈工作，也要为人们分享真实感受创造空间。如果你注意到某人总是有所保留、渐渐沉默、或在会议上不贡献，就温和而带支持地提出来。这些对话表明你在乎、表明你关注的不只是产出；它们帮人们感到被看见、被倾听。

— PDF p.210 —

You can also use tools like the Psychological Safety Ladder Canvas that can help your team visualize how safe team members feel and where support is needed.

你还可以使用诸如“心理安全阶梯画布”（Psychological Safety Ladder Canvas）之类的工具，帮团队可视化成员们感到有多安全、以及哪里需要支持。

Encouraging collaboration also greatly contributes to psychological safety, as it builds trust, mutual respect, and shared ownership. More on this in the section “Enabling Collaboration Inside the Team” on page 209.

鼓励协作也会大大促进心理安全感，因为它能建立信任、相互尊重和共同拥有。详见第 209 页“促进团队内部协作”一节。

By showing vulnerability, encouraging open discussions, and encouraging a learning mindset, you create the foundation for a strong, positive culture.

通过展现脆弱、鼓励开放讨论、并倡导学习型心态，你就在为一种强大而积极的文化打下基础。

What Happens When Psychological Safety Is Lost失去心理安全感会怎样

As hard as psychological safety is to build, it's incredibly easy to lose. You can spend months creating a safe environment, only to undo it in a moment. I've experienced this firsthand.

心理安全感建立起来难，失去却异常容易。你可以花几个月营造一个安全的环境，却可能在一瞬间把它毁掉。我对此有切身经历。

I was part of a team that felt genuinely close; we were collaborative, positive, and high-performing. We had been working together for a while, and we had a strong bond with our tech lead and good rapport with leadership. Everything felt solid.

我曾身处一支关系真正亲密的团队；我们协作、积极、高绩效。我们已经共事了一段时间，与技术负责人关系牢固、与领导层也相处融洽。一切看起来都很稳。

Then one day, without warning, one of our team members was let go. No heads-up, no context, just that it was a “performance issue” and she had to leave immediately. The effect on the team was instant. Suddenly, it didn't feel like any of us were safe. People grew anxious, worried about their own performance, and afraid to speak up. Trust was shaken. The openness we had built disappeared almost overnight.

然后有一天，毫无预兆地，我们的一位成员被裁了。没有提前打招呼、没有说明背景，只说是“绩效问题”，她必须立刻离开。对团队的影响是即时的。突然间，我们谁都觉得不安全了。人们变得焦虑，开始担心自己的表现，不敢再发声。信任被动摇。我们辛辛苦苦建立起来的开放，几乎一夜之间消失了。

Whether or not the decision was justified isn't the point. How it was handled sent a message: you're replaceable, and no one will tell you why. Morale dropped. Engagement dropped. And it took us months to feel like a team again.

那个决定是否合理，并不是重点。重点是它处理的方式传递了一个信号：你是可以被替换的，而且没人会告诉你为什么。士气跌落了，投入度跌落了。我们花了好几个月，才重新找回团队的感觉。

You can think of trust like social capital: every respectful interaction, supportive gesture, or fair decision adds to your balance. But it takes only one misstep, like ignoring team input or showing bias, to make a significant withdrawal. The more capital you build, the more resilient your team becomes. But the account is never infinite.

你可以把信任想象成社会资本：每一次尊重的互动、支持的举动、或公正的决策，都在为你的余额存款。但只需一次失误——比如无视团队意见、或表现出偏见——就会发生一笔大额支取。你积累的资本越多，团队就越有韧性。但这个账户永远不是无限的。

One of the quickest ways to damage psychological safety is through discrimination, even in subtle forms like microaggressions. Things like a casual joke or an offhand comment can land harder than you realize. They don't need to be overt to do harm. Culture is shaped by small, everyday actions, not grand gestures. So reflect on your own biases, stay aware of how your words affect others, and speak up when something feels off. If someone on your team is affected by bias or exclusion, check in with them. A quiet acknowledgment can mean more than you think.

破坏心理安全感最快的方式之一，就是歧视——哪怕是微歧视这种微妙形式。一个随口的玩笑、一句不经意的评论，造成的伤害可能比你意识到的更重。它们不必是明目张胆的，也足以造成伤害。文化是由日常的小举动、而不是宏大姿态塑造的。所以要反思你自己的偏见、留意你的话如何影响他人、并在感觉不对劲时发声。如果团队里有人因偏见或排斥而受到影响，去关心一下他们。一句轻声的体谅，可能比你想的更有分量。

— PDF p.211 —

Mistakes will happen, and will happen to you too. What matters most is how you respond. A simple, sincere apology goes much further than a defensive explanation. Avoid phrases like “I didn't mean to offend you” or “It was just a joke”; intent doesn't erase impact. Acknowledge the harm, take ownership, and show that you're committed to doing better. And when you witness something inappropriate, even a quiet “Hey, that didn't sit right with me” can help uphold the team's values.

错误总会发生，也会发生在你自己身上。最重要的是你如何回应。一句简单、真诚的道歉，远比一番辩解式的解释更有用。避免说“我不是有意冒犯你”或“这只是个玩笑”这类话；意图并不能抹去造成的影响。承认伤害、承担责任、并表明你决心做得更好。而当你目睹不当言行时，哪怕只是轻声一句“哎，我听着有点不舒服”，也有助于维护团队的价值观。

Unconscious bias exists in all of us. As a tech lead, these biases can show up in how you assign work, who you go to for input, or whose ideas you elevate, often without you realizing it. For example, you might find yourself more frequently connecting with people who share similar backgrounds or communication styles. While this is human, it's important to recognize the pattern. Even subtle imbalances can lead to a perception of favoritism, which erodes trust.

我们每个人身上都存在无意识偏见。作为技术负责人，这些偏见可能体现在你如何分派工作、你向谁征求意见、或你抬举谁的想法上——而且往往是你自己没意识到的。例如，你可能发现自己更常与那些背景或沟通风格相似的人交流。虽然这是人之常情，但认清这种模式很重要。哪怕是微妙的失衡，也可能让人觉得你偏心，从而侵蚀信任。

To keep yourself in check, make a habit of gathering feedback from everyone on the team, especially from quieter members. Staying self-aware, questioning your patterns, and striving to be fair in every interaction are essential to maintaining a culture of psychological safety.

为了自我检视，养成向团队每个人收集反馈的习惯，尤其是那些较安静的成员。保持自我觉察、质疑自己的行为模式、并在每一次互动中力求公平，对于维持心理安全文化至关重要。

How to Evaluate if Your Team Is High-Performing如何评估你的团队是否高绩效

High performance is more of an aim than a goal. It's about continuously pushing and striving to do better as a team. It's about continuously checking that you are on the right track. It's not something you can check completely off your list: you cannot get to a point where you say, “I have a high-performing team. It's done.” Even when you get there, it takes continuous effort to keep the high standards.

高绩效与其说是一个目标，不如说是一个方向。它关乎作为一个团队不断推动、力求做得更好。它关乎不断确认自己走在正确的轨道上。它不是你能从清单上彻底划掉的东西：你不可能到达某个节点后说“我有了一支高绩效团队，大功告成。”即便你到了那里，也需要持续付出努力去维持高标准。

You can't improve what you don't measure. But when it comes to evaluating things like psychological safety, collaboration, or trust, the metrics become more nuanced.

你无法改进你不去衡量的东西。但当要评估心理安全感、协作或信任这类事物时，指标就变得更微妙了。

There are well-known frameworks and tools that attempt to measure engineering team performance, such as the following:

有一些知名的框架和工具试图衡量工程团队的绩效，例如：

  • DORA (DevOps Research and Assessment) — Focuses on deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, and time to recovery. It's commonly used to assess software delivery performance.DORA（DevOps 研究与评估）—— 聚焦部署频率、变更前置时间、变更失败率和恢复时间。常用于评估软件交付绩效。
  • SPACE framework — A more holistic model that includes dimensions like satisfaction and well-being, performance, activity, communication and collaboration, and efficiency and flow.SPACE 框架 —— 一个更整体的模型，包含满意度与福祉、绩效、活动量、沟通与协作、以及效率与心流等维度。
  • Accelerate framework — Closely tied to DORA, it provides research-backed insights into what drives high-performing engineering teams, with a focus on lean product development and DevOps practices.Accelerate 框架 —— 与 DORA 紧密相关，它为“是什么驱动高绩效工程团队”提供有研究支撑的洞见，聚焦精益产品开发和 DevOps 实践。
— PDF p.212 —

While none are perfect, it's useful to be familiar with them, as they may be referenced in your organization.

虽然没有一个是完美的，但熟悉它们是有用的，因为你的组织可能会引用它们。

These tools can be valuable, but they often require investment in data gathering, processes, and consistent interpretation. In the meantime, there are simpler, more qualitative signals you can use to evaluate how your team is doing and where you might improve:

这些工具很有价值，但它们往往需要在数据采集、流程和持续解读上投入。与此同时，你可以用一些更简单、更定性的信号，来评估团队现状以及可以改进之处：

  • Your own observations — Start with regular reflection. Amid the pace of delivery, it's easy to overlook signs of drift or tension. Block time to ask yourself, “What feels off in the team right now?,” “What would I change if I could?,” or “Is everyone contributing equally in meetings?” Look for quiet voices, disengagement, or recurring topics in one-on-ones or retrospectives that might point to deeper issues.你自己的观察 —— 从定期反思开始。在交付的快节奏中，很容易忽略跑偏或紧张的迹象。留出时间问问自己：“团队现在哪里感觉不对劲？”“如果可以，我会改变什么？”“会议上每个人都在平等贡献吗？”留意那些安静的声音、 disengaged 的状态，或一对一面谈/复盘中反复出现、可能指向更深问题的话题。
  • Team feedback — But don't rely on only your own lens; your interpretation could be biased or incomplete. Always bring these reflections into conversation with your team. Ask the team directly how they feel about working together. Retrospectives, one-on-ones, and anonymous surveys are all useful entry points. Go beyond surface-level questions. Instead of asking, “How do you think we're doing?” try “What's one thing we could improve about how we collaborate?” or “When do you feel most included or excluded in this team?” Use this feedback to validate or challenge your own assumptions.团队反馈 —— 但不要只依赖你自己的视角；你的解读可能有偏差或不完整。一定要把这些反思带到与团队的对话中。直接问团队：大家觉得协作得怎么样？复盘、一对一面谈、匿名问卷都是有用的切入点。不要停留在表面问题上。与其问“你觉得我们做得怎么样？”，不如试试“在协作方式上，有哪一点我们可以改进？”或“在这个团队里，你什么时候最感到被包容、什么时候最感到被排斥？”用这些反馈去验证或挑战你自己的假设。
  • Stakeholder feedback — External recognition is one of the clearest signs of a high-performing team. When stakeholders, whether PMs, execs, or other teams, trust you, they'll show it. That might look like positive, unsolicited feedback about your impact, stakeholders referencing your work to others, or being entrusted with high-visibility or critical projects. If external praise is rare or vague, it could mean the team's value isn't well understood, or not as strong as it should be.干系人反馈 —— 外部认可是高绩效团队最清晰的标志之一。当干系人——无论是产品经理、高管还是其他团队——信任你时，他们会表现出来。这可能体现为主动送上门的、关于你影响力的正面反馈，或他们向别人提起你的工作，或把高关注度、关键的项目交给你。如果外部的赞扬稀少或含糊，可能意味着团队的价值没有被充分理解，或没有它应有的那么强。
  • Reputation and interest — When your team is truly high-performing, others want to work with you. People will ask to join your team, shadow how you work, or borrow your practices. In my team, we saw this when engineers from other projects reached out for advice or expressed interest in rotating onto our team.口碑与兴趣 —— 当你的团队真正高绩效时，别人会想和你共事。人们会申请加入你的团队、观摩你们如何工作、或借鉴你们的做法。在我的团队里，当其他项目的工程师主动来请教、或表达想轮岗加入我们团队时，我们就看到了这一点。
  • Engagement and ownership — Another good indicator is engagement. Are team members bringing energy and initiative to problems? Do they raise issues without being asked, follow through on commitments, and hold each other accountable? Or do you have to follow up repeatedly just to maintain momentum? A team's internal motivation is one of the most telling signs of its health.投入与担当 —— 另一个好指标是投入度。团队成员面对问题时是否带来活力和主动性？他们是否不用别人催就主动提出问题、兑现承诺、并互相督促？还是说，你得反复跟进才能维持势头？一个团队的内在动力，是其健康状况最有力的信号之一。
  • Results and standards — Of course, performance also shows up in outcomes. Are you delivering what's expected? Are you hitting quality benchmarks? But results alone don't tell the whole story. It's the consistency, the collaboration, and the trust behind those results that really matter.结果与标准 —— 当然，绩效也会体现在成果上。你们交付了预期的东西吗？达到质量基准了吗？但光看结果并不能说明全貌。真正重要的，是结果背后的一致性、协作和信任。
— PDF p.213 —

High performance is an ongoing pursuit. You don't “arrive” at having a high-performing team. Even once you've built one, it takes constant care to maintain. Priorities shift, people change, and new challenges emerge. Nobody out there has a team that's 100% high-performing, 100% of the time, and that's OK. Teams go through ups and downs, and part of your role as a tech lead is to keep checking the pulse, respond with empathy, and continually adjust.

高绩效是一场持续的追求。你不会“抵达”高绩效团队的终点。即便你建成了一支，也需要不断呵护才能维持。优先级会变、人会变、新的挑战会冒出来。世上没有人拥有一支 100% 高绩效、且 100% 时间都如此的团队，而这没关系。团队会经历起伏；作为技术负责人，你的部分职责就是不断把脉、带着同理心理应、并持续调整。

How to Approach Performance Reviews如何应对绩效评估

The goal of performance reviews is to have people reflect on their overall performance from the previous six months or one year and to give raises and promotions. It's also an opportunity to have people reflect on where they want to go and where they are and identify gaps in their skills and create a plan to address them. It's a chance to get feedback and give feedback, but it should not replace timely feedback (more on this in Chapter 5).

绩效评估的目标，是让人们回顾过去半年或一年的整体表现，并据此调薪和晋升。它也是一个机会，让人们思考自己想去哪里、现在身处何处，找出技能上的缺口、并制定弥补计划。它是获得反馈和给出反馈的契机，但不应取代及时的反馈（更多见第 5 章）。

— PDF p.214 —

Based on your company structure and culture, your role in performance reviews for your team might be different. Some tech leads are barely involved in the performance review process for their team, as they are not expected to be involved. Other roles, like team leads or engineering managers, will take care of the heavy lifting of the process of review and growth.

根据公司结构和文化的不同，你在团队绩效评估中的角色可能有所差异。有些技术负责人几乎不参与团队的绩效评估流程，因为本就不指望他们参与。另一些角色，比如团队负责人或工程经理，则会扛起评估与成长流程中的重活。

And there are companies where you, as a tech lead, play a key role in the performance review process, given that the team lead role overlaps with your role and the engineering manager has a more high-level approach in the process.

还有一些公司里，你作为技术负责人会在绩效评估流程中扮演关键角色——因为团队负责人的角色与你的角色重叠，而工程经理在流程中采取更宏观的方式。

My personal opinion is that the tech lead should play a key role in reviewing the performance of their team members, helping them build a case for promotion and acting as a supporter or cheerleader in front of management, or giving honest feedback when someone isn't meeting expectations. Who better to know about people's performance than you, who work daily side by side with them on technical and nontechnical topics?

我个人的看法是：技术负责人应当在评估团队成员表现上扮演关键角色，帮他们准备晋升的论据、在管理层面前做他们的支持者和啦啦队，或在某人未达期望时给出坦诚的反馈。还有谁比每天与他们并肩处理技术与非技术事务的你，更了解大家的表现呢？

Also, as a tech lead, I want to have a say in my team members' growth and development and do everything in my power to support them, as that will highly impact the overall performance of my team and, of course, me.

此外，作为技术负责人，我希望对团队成员的成长与发展有发言权，并尽我所能支持他们，因为这会深刻影响我团队的整体绩效，当然，也包括我自己。

I have always been a key player in the performance review process for my team members, and this is the case that I will prepare you for in the next sections. I'll cover how to ensure everyone is aligned on the process and is fully making use of it, how to support them in the process, how to use different tools to measure performance, and what to do with the results.

我自己一直是团队成员绩效评估流程中的关键角色，接下来的小节也会按这种情形为你做准备。我会讲到：如何确保每个人都对齐流程、并充分利用它；如何在流程中支持他们；如何使用不同工具衡量绩效；以及拿到结果后该做什么。

But before we dive into supporting others, let's start with your own review process. Learning how to manage your own review well will help you better understand the system, set the right tone, and apply the same principles when guiding your team.

但在我们深入讲如何支持他人之前，先从你自己的评估流程说起。学会管好自己的评估，会帮你更好地理解这套体系、定下正确的基调，并在指导团队时运用同样的原则。

How to Prepare for Your Own Performance Review如何准备自己的绩效评估

Your own performance review is the first process you need to manage. Leading by example will not only make it easier to guide your team through the process but also help you refine how you approach it. Instead of just telling them how to prepare, you'll be able to show them.

你自己的绩效评估，是你需要先管好的第一个流程。以身作则不仅会让你更容易引导团队走过这个流程，还会帮你完善自己应对它的方式。你不只是告诉他们该怎么准备，更能亲自做给他们看。

Get clarity on the process先搞清楚流程

Start by understanding how performance reviews work in your company. What are the timelines, expectations, and key steps? Who is involved, what tools are used, and how is progress tracked? Who makes the decisions, and who can support you? Some companies, like Thoughtworks, have the role of performance partners that act as mentors and advocate for your growth. Identify the people who can help you navigate this process, and make sure they are aware of your plans.

先了解你们公司的绩效评估是怎么运作的。时间线、期望、关键步骤是什么？有哪些人参与、用什么工具、进展如何跟踪？谁做决策、谁能支持你？有些公司，比如 Thoughtworks，设有“绩效伙伴”（performance partner）这一角色，充当导师并为你的成长发声。找出能帮你走通这个流程的人，并确保他们了解你的计划。

— PDF p.215 —

Gather all available documentation and list anything unclear. Then, go back to your manager to clarify assumptions and questions. Role expectations documents can also be useful, as they help you understand how performance is evaluated at different levels.

收集所有能找到的文档，把不清楚的地方列出来。然后回到经理那里，澄清你的假设和疑问。角色期望文档也很有用，它能帮你理解不同层级的绩效是如何评估的。

Once you have a clear understanding of the process, create a plan: define the actions you need to take, who you need feedback from, and how you will track everything. Many companies provide tools to collect and visualize feedback, but if yours doesn't, a simple spreadsheet will do.

一旦你对流程有了清晰理解，就制定一份计划：明确你需要采取的行动、需要向谁征求反馈、以及你将如何跟踪这一切。很多公司提供收集和可视化反馈的工具；如果你们没有，一个简单的电子表格就够了。

Define what you want明确你想要什么

What do you expect from your next performance review? Maybe you're aiming for a salary raise, a grade change, or opportunities to develop specific skills and connections. For example, I got most of my leadership training through a performance review cycle. I researched internal leadership programs and built a strong case for why I should be part of them, highlighting how they aligned with my development and the value I could bring back to the company.

你希望从下一次绩效评估中得到什么？也许你瞄准的是加薪、职级调整，或发展特定技能与人脉的机会。例如，我大部分的领导力培训，都是通过一轮绩效评估争取来的。我调研了内部的领导力项目，并为“我为什么应该加入”构建了有力论据，强调它们如何与我的发展对齐、以及我能为公司带回什么价值。

Be specific about your goals. Whether it's getting a mentor, working on a particular skill, or connecting with peers in similar roles, having a clear ask increases your chances of getting what you want.

目标要具体。无论你是想要一位导师、打磨某项特定技能，还是与同岗位的人建立联系，有一个清晰的诉求，都会提高你得偿所愿的概率。

Build your lists列出你的清单

Start by listing what you're proud of, the impact you've had. As a tech lead, it's not just about your individual contributions anymore. Your success is measured by your team's success. Shift from “I delivered this feature” to “I helped Alan improve his soft skills through mentoring” or “I unblocked the team on an initiative by facilitating key conversations.” Think about how you've enabled your team to do their best work.

先列出你引以为豪的事、你产生的影响。作为技术负责人，这不再只关乎你个人的贡献。你的成功是以团队的成功来衡量的。把视角从“我交付了这个功能”转向“我通过带教帮 Alan 提升了软技能”，或“我通过促成关键对话，为团队在某个举措上解除了阻塞”。想想你是如何让团队做到最好的。

Note — Consider keeping a running “brag document,” as recommended by Julia Evans. It's a simple practice: maintain a private doc where you jot down accomplishments as they happen. That way, when review season rolls around, you're not starting from scratch, and you're less likely to forget the small, important wins.

注——可以考虑按 Julia Evans 的建议，维护一份持续更新的“自夸文档”（brag document）。做法很简单：建一份私人文档，一有成就就随手记下。这样当评估季到来时，你就不必从零开始，也更不容易忘记那些小小的、却重要的胜利。

— PDF p.216 —

Just as relevant as accomplishments are the challenges you've faced. The best learning often comes from things that went wrong. That's why postmortems exist, because reflecting on failures helps us improve. The same applies to performance reviews. Managers don't just want to hear that everything is great. They want to see growth and how you've handled setbacks, missed deadlines, skill gaps, and difficult situations. Take a look at what's happened since your last review: major milestones, wins, struggles, incidents, and feedback you've received. Use these to build a well-rounded view of your progress.

与成就同样重要的，是你经历过的挑战。最好的学习往往来自出过错的事。这正是复盘存在的意义——反思失败帮我们改进。绩效评估也是同理。管理者不只想听到“一切都好”。他们想看到成长，看到你如何应对挫折、错过的截止日期、技能缺口和困难局面。回顾一下自上次评估以来发生了什么：重要里程碑、胜利、挣扎、事故、以及你收到的反馈。用这些来构建一个关于你进展的、完整立体的图景。

Make sure your accomplishments and challenges align with the expectations of your role. Many tech leads never revisit their job description; they simply assume they know what's expected. This mismatch often leads to frustration when aiming for promotions, as what they consider valuable may not align with what the organization or leadership is actually looking for.

确保你的成就和挑战与岗位期望对齐。很多技术负责人从不回头看自己的岗位描述；他们只是默认自己知道期望是什么。这种错位常常在争取晋升时带来挫败，因为他们自认为有价值的东西，可能与组织或领导层真正看重的并不一致。

For instance, some tech leads believe their main responsibility is only dealing with every technical challenge their team faces. As a result, they spend most of their time staying up-to-date on technologies and reviewing code while neglecting critical responsibilities like mentoring team members, enabling growth, or collaborating with product managers to shape a strategic roadmap. These overlooked areas are often exactly what the organization expects from someone in a leadership position. So, to avoid any bad surprises, make sure to validate your lists against the official role description and in conversation with your manager before moving forward. You can find more on this topic in the section “Understanding the Expectations of Your Role” on page 12.

例如，有些技术负责人认为自己的主要职责只是处理团队面对的每一个技术挑战。结果，他们把大部分时间花在跟进技术动态和 review 代码上，却忽视了带教团队成员、促成成长、或与产品经理协作制定战略路线图等关键职责。而这些被忽视的领域，往往恰恰是组织对一个身居领导岗位者的期望。因此，为避免任何意外，在推进之前，务必对照官方岗位描述、并在与经理的谈话中核实你的清单。关于这个话题，详见第 12 页“理解你岗位的期望”一节。

Once you have your accomplishments and challenges, combine them into a cohesive narrative. Show how your wins and struggles contributed to your growth as a tech lead and the overall success of the team.

一旦你列好了成就和挑战，就把它们整合成一个连贯的叙事。展现你的胜利与挣扎如何促成了你作为技术负责人的成长、以及团队的整体成功。

Ask for feedback征求反馈

Feedback is a critical part of any performance review. You'll likely need input from your team, managers, and stakeholders. As a tech lead, this feedback is even more required because your performance is heavily influenced by how others perceive your leadership.

反馈是任何绩效评估的关键组成部分。你很可能需要来自团队、经理和干系人的意见。作为技术负责人，这种反馈更加必要，因为你的绩效很大程度上取决于别人如何看待你的领导。

I've seen tech leads struggle because they felt they were doing poorly when their team actually thought otherwise or were caught off guard by unexpected feedback because they weren't checking in regularly. It's easy to misjudge your own impact when you don't have external perspectives. (For a detailed process on how to collect and use feedback effectively, check out Chapter 5.)

我见过技术负责人很挣扎：他们以为自己做得不好，而团队其实并不这么看；又或者因为平时不常同步，被意外的反馈打了个措手不及。当你缺乏外部视角时，很容易误判自己的影响。（关于如何有效收集和使用反馈的详细流程，见第 5 章。）

Use the feedback to refine your accomplishments and challenges lists.

用这些反馈去打磨你的成就清单和挑战清单。

— PDF p.217 —

Feedback is valuable only if you follow up on it. Have conversations to clarify points, gather additional examples, and resolve inconsistencies. Sometimes, different team members will have conflicting views of your role. Juniors may expect you to code more, while seniors appreciate that you focus on strategy and alignment. Understanding these perspectives will help you address concerns and set expectations.

反馈只有在你跟进之后才有价值。通过对话澄清要点、补充更多例子、化解不一致。有时，不同团队成员对你的角色会有相互冲突的看法。初级者可能期望你多写代码，而资深者则欣赏你专注于战略和对齐。理解这些视角，会帮你回应顾虑、并设定期望。

Make your work visible让你的工作被看见

Use every opportunity in the review process to advocate for yourself and your team. Even if something is optional, consider doing it anyway.

在评估流程中，利用一切机会为你自己和你的团队发声。哪怕某件事是可选的，也不妨去做。

At Thoughtworks, we had an optional presentation phase where people could present their case to senior leadership. Many skipped it because it wasn't required, but I always did it. It gave me a rare opportunity to tell my story, clearly state what I wanted, and address any concerns directly. Senior leadership taking the time to attend these sessions was a sign of great leadership in itself. These presentations didn't just impact my performance review; they helped build relationships with decision makers that benefited my career long term.

在 Thoughtworks，我们有一个可选的展示环节，人们可以向高层领导陈述自己的情况。很多人因为不是强制就跳过了，但我每次都做。它给了我一个难得的机会去讲述自己的故事、清晰说出我想要什么、并直接回应任何顾虑。高层领导愿意花时间参加这些环节，本身就是优秀领导力的体现。这些展示不仅影响了我的绩效评估，还帮我与决策者建立了关系，让我的职业生涯长期受益。

Performance reviews are a powerful opportunity to reflect on your impact, advocate for your growth, and shape your development path. As a tech lead, how you approach them influences your own progress and sets the tone for how your team engages with the process too.

绩效评估是一个有力的契机，让你反思自己的影响、为成长发声、并塑造自己的发展路径。作为技术负责人，你如何对待它，既影响你自己的进展，也为团队如何参与这个流程定下基调。

How to Help Your Team Prepare for Their Reviews如何帮助团队准备绩效评估

Now that you've seen how to manage your own performance review, it's time to apply that same mindset to supporting your team. Many of the steps, like reflecting on achievements, gathering feedback, and clarifying goals, overlap, but your role shifts. Instead of advocating for yourself, you're now helping others do the same.

既然你已经看到如何管好自己的绩效评估，现在就该把同样的心态用于支持团队了。许多步骤——回顾成就、收集反馈、澄清目标——是重叠的，但你的角色变了。你不再是为自己发声，而是帮别人去做同样的事。

As a tech lead, you play a key role in the performance review process, not just in guiding your team through it but also in evaluating their work. Your assessment carries weight, so it's essential to approach this process with intention and clarity.

作为技术负责人，你在绩效评估流程中扮演关键角色——不仅是引导团队走过流程，还包括评估他们的工作。你的评估是有分量的，因此带着意图和清晰去对待这个流程至关重要。

If you're new to a team and have to conduct performance reviews without much historical context, acknowledge this up front. Let both your team and your manager know that your insights may be limited. In some cases, tech leads ask their engineering manager to handle the formal review while they focus on helping their team reflect on accomplishments and future goals. Even if you're not the final decision maker, you should still facilitate meaningful discussions to help your team navigate the process effectively.

如果你刚加入一个团队、且不得不在缺乏历史背景的情况下做绩效评估，就 upfront 承认这一点。让团队和经理都知道，你的见解可能有限。在某些情况下，技术负责人会请工程经理负责正式评估，自己则专注于帮团队回顾成就和未来目标。即便你不是最终决策者，也仍应促成有意义的讨论，帮团队高效地走完这个流程。

— PDF p.218 —

Set the right mindset树立正确的心态

First, make sure your team understands why performance reviews matter. Many techies see them as just another task to check off the list, missing opportunities to showcase their work, get valuable feedback, and advocate for growth. Without proper guidance, they often scramble to collect feedback last minute, leading to unnecessary stress and missed chances for meaningful recognition.

首先，确保团队理解绩效评估为什么重要。很多技术人把它当成又一项打勾了事的任务，白白错失了展示工作、获得宝贵反馈、为成长发声的机会。没有恰当引导，他们往往在最后一刻才手忙脚乱地收集反馈，导致不必要的压力，以及获得有意义认可的机会流失。

Take the time to communicate the purpose of the review process and how it impacts promotions, salary increases, and professional development. Clarify expectations, timelines, and what happens after the review. People are more likely to take the process seriously when they understand its value.

花时间讲清楚评估流程的目的，以及它如何影响晋升、加薪和职业发展。澄清期望、时间线、以及评估之后会发生什么。当人们理解了它的价值，就更可能认真对待这个流程。

Make the process smoother让流程更顺畅

You can help reduce the friction of performance reviews by integrating them into your team's workflow well in advance. Plan ahead and factor in the time required for feedback collection, reflection, and discussions. This period will inevitably impact your team's delivery, so acknowledge that and adjust roadmaps accordingly. Keeping stakeholders informed of this impact helps manage expectations.

你可以通过提前把绩效评估融入团队工作流，来降低它的摩擦。提前规划，把收集反馈、反思和讨论所需的时间考虑进去。这段时期不可避免地会影响团队的交付，因此要承认这一点、并相应调整路线图。让干系人了解这种影响，有助于管理预期。

Make sure everyone knows the steps, roles, and responsibilities involved. Be clear about your role, what decisions you influence, what is outside your control, and how much weight your input carries. Ensure your team has access to all the necessary resources, templates, and tools, and encourage them to start preparing early. One-on-ones are a great way to bring up performance review prep gradually instead of dumping everything on them last minute.

确保每个人都知道涉及的步骤、角色和责任。讲清楚你的角色、你能影响哪些决策、哪些不在你的掌控之内、以及你的意见有多大分量。确保团队能用上所有必要的资源、模板和工具，并鼓励他们提早开始准备。一对一面谈是一个好途径，可以循序渐进地提起绩效评估准备，而不是在最后一刻把一堆事砸给他们。

Encourage your team members to think about their expectations for the process. Are they aiming for a promotion, a salary increase, or feedback on their growth? The earlier they articulate this, the better you can support them. If someone expects a 10% raise but the company's maximum is 5%, setting that expectation early prevents frustration. If someone is striving for a senior role, you can gather examples of when they demonstrated leadership or took initiative to strengthen their case.

鼓励团队成员想清楚他们对这个流程的期望。他们是瞄准晋升、加薪，还是关于成长的反馈？他们越早把这一点说清楚，你就越能支持他们。如果有人期望加薪 10%、而公司上限是 5%，早点把这个期望讲清楚能避免挫败。如果有人在争取高级岗位，你可以收集他们展现领导力或主动担当的事例，来强化他们的论据。

— PDF p.219 —

Give effective feedback给出有效的反馈

Don't leave your feedback until the last minute. Some companies use automated tools for performance reviews, while others rely on individuals to gather input manually. Regardless of the system, aim to submit your feedback early and include specific examples. This not only strengthens your team's self-assessments but also gives them more insights into their own performance.

不要把反馈拖到最后一刻。有些公司用自动化工具做绩效评估，另一些则靠个人手动收集意见。无论用哪种体系，都尽量早点提交反馈、并附上具体事例。这不仅能强化团队的自我评估，也能让他们对自己的表现有更多洞察。

Before finalizing your evaluations, have one-on-one conversations with each team member. Go over your feedback together, highlight areas of agreement, and discuss any discrepancies. This reduces the risk of unpleasant surprises where people might read something later in your feedback they were not aware of.

在敲定评估之前，与每位团队成员分别做一次一对一面谈。一起过一遍你的反馈，标出达成一致的地方，讨论任何不一致之处。这能降低那种令人不快的意外风险——即人们在你的反馈里读到了自己事先并不知情的内容。

Keep the process moving推动流程前进

Use your one-on-ones to check in on progress and ensure people are actively reflecting on their work, gathering feedback, and preparing their reviews. Running feedback-focused sessions, like Speedback (covered in the section “Building a Feedback Culture on Your Team” on page 132), can also help jump-start the process.

利用一对一面谈检查进展，确保大家在积极反思自己的工作、收集反馈、准备评估。组织一些以反馈为核心的环节，比如 Speedback（见第 132 页“在团队中建立反馈文化”一节），也能帮这个流程快速启动。

If you've been tracking team milestones and feedback throughout the year (as recommended in the previous section), this is the time to revisit those notes. Use them to remind people of their accomplishments and challenges, helping them build a more complete picture of their growth.

如果你一整年都在跟踪团队的里程碑和反馈（如前面小节所建议的），现在就是重温这些笔记的时候。用它们提醒大家自己的成就和挑战，帮他们为自己的成长构建一幅更完整的图景。

Help your team evaluate themselves帮团队做自我评价

One of the most impactful ways you can support your team during performance reviews as a tech lead is by helping them evaluate themselves with honesty and clarity.

作为技术负责人，在绩效评估期间支持团队的最有力方式之一，就是帮他们以诚实和清晰来评估自己。

A great starting point is your company's official role descriptions or skills matrix. Use these as a shared reference to guide your conversations. Ask each team member to self-assess across the different expectations, either for their current role or the one they're aiming for. This will surface strengths, reveal growth areas, and help set a common foundation.

一个很好的起点是公司官方的岗位描述或技能矩阵。把它们作为共同参照来引导你们的对话。请每位团队成员针对不同的期望做自评——无论是对当前岗位、还是对他们瞄准的目标岗位。这会凸显长处、揭示成长空间，并帮你们建立共同基础。

A 1–10 scale can be a useful tool here but only if used intentionally. Have them rate themselves across the relevant competencies, and then ask, “Why did you choose that number?” This simple question often unlocks insights they hadn't fully articulated. For team members who tend to undersell their contributions, walking through real examples can help them realize they're further along than they thought. For others, the conversation might highlight blind spots or the need to gather better evidence to support their self-assessment.

1 到 10 的评分在这里可以是个有用的工具，但前提是刻意地使用。请他们针对相关能力给自己打分，然后问：“你为什么选这个数字？”这个简单的问题往往能打开他们此前未曾完整表达的洞见。对于那些往往低估自己贡献的成员，一起过一遍真实事例，能帮他们意识到自己比想象中走得更远。对另一些人，这场对话可能会暴露盲点、或表明需要收集更好的证据来支撑其自评。

Then ask, “What would make this a 10?” This helps define what success looks like in practical terms. If you can't describe a 10, how will you know when you've arrived? I once had a junior engineer say their “10” in technical skills meant “being the best Scala developer on the team.” But as she said it out loud, she realized that wasn't realistic, or necessary. She redefined it to something more grounded: “Being able to deliver a feature end to end in our Scala service on time and with minimal support.”

然后问：“怎么做才能到 10？”这有助于在实际层面定义成功长什么样。如果你描述不出一个 10，又怎么知道自己何时抵达？我曾有一位初级工程师说，她在技术能力上的“10”意味着“成为团队里最厉害的 Scala 开发”。但当她把这句话说出口时，她意识到那既不现实、也无必要。她把它重新定义成一个更踏实的目标：“能在我们的 Scala 服务里，按时、并在最少的支持下端到端交付一个功能。”

— PDF p.220 —

Some people hesitate to ever rate themselves a 9 or 10, even when they meet the bar, because they fear appearing arrogant. I often say, “If you're never going to use a 10, why have it on the scale?” Or “Why should they promote you if you are not exceeding expectations in any area?” This might sound harsh at first but it usually triggers a shift in mindset, helping people assess themselves fairly.

有些人即便达到了标准，也羞于给自己打 9 或 10，因为怕显得自大。我常说：“如果你永远不打算用 10，那刻度上留着它干嘛？”或者：“如果你在任何一个领域都没有超出期望，他们凭什么晋升你？”这话乍听可能有点狠，但它通常会触发心态的转变，帮人们公正地评估自己。

Disclosure: this process isn't really about the numbers. It's about the clarity and reflection that come from justifying them and using that insight to shape what comes next.

说明：这个过程其实并不关乎数字本身。它关乎“为数字找理由”所带来的清晰与反思，以及用这份洞察去塑造接下来的路。

Sometimes, you and a team member might not see eye to eye, especially when it comes to promotions. For example, many developers, especially at the senior level, fall into the trap of thinking that technical improvement is all that matters. But being a senior developer goes far beyond writing excellent code. It often includes mentoring others, leading initiatives, owning outcomes, collaborating effectively across departments, and demonstrating accountability. If a team member is focused only on developing their coding skills while working in a silo, they're missing key parts of their role, and that can hold them back.

有时，你和某位团队成员可能看法不一致，尤其是在晋升这件事上。例如，很多开发者——尤其是高级别——会掉进一个陷阱：以为技术提升才是唯一重要的事。但做一名高级开发，远不止是写出优秀的代码。它往往还包括带教他人、牵头举措、对结果负责、跨部门高效协作、以及展现担当。如果一位团队成员只专注于打磨编码技能、却在孤岛里工作，那他正在错过自己角色的关键部分，而这会拖他的后腿。

These conversations can feel personal or even tense, but the solution is to move away from subjective opinions and focus on shared criteria. Refer back to the company's expectations and ask: What behaviors are visible today? What impact are they having? If they feel ready and you don't, walk through the expectations together. Point to concrete examples of where they meet them and where growth is still needed.

这些对话可能让人觉得触及个人、甚至紧张，但解法是摆脱主观意见、聚焦共同标准。回到公司的期望，问：今天能看到哪些行为？它们产生了什么影响？如果他们觉得自己准备好了、而你不这么认为，就一起过一遍期望。指出他们在哪里达到了、哪里仍需成长的具体例子。

Handled well, this becomes a constructive, collaborative conversation. It's not “your opinion versus theirs.” You're working together to evaluate what success looks like and how to get there. I've seen this go wrong when the only feedback someone receives is “I just don't feel you're there yet.” That's when frustration and defensiveness take over. If you instead offer specific examples and show the path forward, most people will be open to, and even grateful for, the clarity.

处理得好，这会变成一场建设性的、协作的对话。它不是“你的意见 vs 他的意见”。你们在一起评估成功长什么样、以及如何抵达。我见过这种事搞砸：当某人收到的唯一反馈是“我就是觉得你还没到那份上”。这时挫败和防备就会占据上风。如果你转而给出具体例子、并展示前进的路径，大多数人会乐于接受这种清晰、甚至对此心怀感激。

Helping your team align their self-perception with the actual expectations of the role is one of the most empowering things you can do as a tech lead. It prepares them not just for performance reviews but for long-term, sustainable growth.

帮团队把自我认知与岗位的真实期望对齐，是你作为技术负责人能做的、最能赋能他人的事情之一。它不仅为他们准备了绩效评估，更为长期、可持续的成长做了铺垫。

— PDF p.221 —

Answer last-minute questions回答最后一刻的提问

As the deadline approaches, expect a spike in last-minute questions and concerns. Keep your calendar slightly more flexible so you can provide guidance, set expectations, and help the team approach the process with clarity and confidence.

随着截止日临近，要预期最后一刻的提问和顾虑会激增。把你的日程安排得略微灵活一些，好提供指导、设定期望、并帮团队带着清晰和信心去面对这个流程。

Helping your team through performance reviews means setting the tone, reducing anxiety, and creating opportunities for growth. By offering support, giving thoughtful feedback, and aligning self-assessments with company standards, you empower them to take ownership of their development and ensure no one is caught off guard when decisions are made.

帮团队走过绩效评估，意味着定下基调、减轻焦虑、并创造成长机会。通过提供支持、给出深思熟虑的反馈、并把自评与公司标准对齐，你赋能他们为自己的成长负责，并确保没有人在决策出炉时措手不及。

What to Do After the Review Conversation评估谈话之后该做什么

At this stage, your involvement becomes more limited, as the formal performance review process typically involves multiple managers. They take a high-level view, considering factors like budget, business priorities, and overall team performance. Their decisions about things like who gets promoted and who gets a raise are based on feedback, assessments, and company objectives.

在这个阶段，你的参与会变得更有限，因为正式的绩效评估流程通常涉及多位经理。他们采取宏观视角，考虑预算、业务优先级和团队整体绩效等因素。他们关于谁晋升、谁加薪的决策，是基于反馈、评估和公司目标做出的。

As a tech lead, you likely won't have the final say on salary adjustments or promotions, but your input carries weight. Since you work closely with the team, your perspective on an individual's readiness for a senior role or their overall contribution will be valuable. Your written feedback is crucial, but expect to be asked by managers for promotion recommendations as well. Your insights can influence outcomes, even if the final decision rests with upper management. Any input you provide in these meetings should reinforce the guidance and expectations you've already communicated.

作为技术负责人，你很可能对调薪或晋升没有最终决定权，但你的意见有分量。因为你与团队紧密共事，你对某人是否胜任高级岗位、或其整体贡献的判断会很有价值。你的书面反馈至关重要，但也要预期经理们会来征求你的晋升推荐。你的洞见可以影响结果，即便最终决定权在高层。你在这些会议中提供的任何意见，都应强化你此前已经传达过的指导和期望。

Once decisions are finalized, the results will be shared with the team. As always, some people will be happy with their outcomes, while others may feel disappointed. Be prepared for follow-up conversations; team members will want to understand what they need to improve and how they can grow.

一旦决策敲定，结果就会告知团队。一如既往，有人会对结果满意，有人可能感到失望。要为后续的谈话做好准备；团队成员会想了解自己需要改进什么、以及如何成长。

The formal review process may end with final decisions and outcome conversations, but your role as a tech lead doesn't stop there. Whether you're supporting someone through a tough result or helping them plan their next growth step, your ongoing involvement is what truly drives development. Don't let the review be the last conversation. This is the perfect time to capture growth plans, while motivation is still high.

正式的评估流程或许以最终决策和结果谈话收尾，但你作为技术负责人的角色并未就此停止。无论你是在陪某个人熬过一个艰难的结果，还是在帮他规划下一步成长，你持续的参与才真正驱动发展。不要让评估成为最后一次对话。趁动力还高，现在正是记录成长计划的最佳时机。

— PDF p.222 —

That means different things for different people:

对不同的人，这意味着不同的事：

  • For those who've recently been promoted into a new role—say, from junior to mid-level or from senior to lead—help them settle into their new responsibilities. Review expectations together, identify stretch opportunities, and find ways for them to develop the new skills they'll need to succeed.对于那些刚晋升到新岗位的人——比如从初级到中级、或从高级到负责人——帮他们适应新职责。一起回顾期望、识别拓展机会、并找到让他们发展成功所需新技能的途径。
  • For high performers or overachievers, don't just say “great job” and move on. Use their enthusiasm as fuel. Look for opportunities to stretch them, delegate impactful projects, and help them grow toward their next goal. This is a great way to keep them engaged and developing.对于高绩效者或超额完成者，不要只说一句“干得漂亮”就翻篇。把他们的热情当作燃料。寻找能拉伸他们的机会，委派有影响力的项目，帮他们朝下一个目标成长。这是保持他们投入和成长的好办法。
  • For someone aiming for a promotion or a role change, work with them to map out a clear development path. Outline what success looks like, what gaps need to be closed, and how you'll support them along the way.对于瞄准晋升或转岗的人，和他们一起规划出一条清晰的发展路径。勾勒成功长什么样、需要补齐哪些缺口、以及一路上你将如何支持他们。
  • For someone flagged as underperforming, you'll need to take a more hands-on approach. Collaborate on a targeted growth plan that addresses the key areas of improvement highlighted in their review. (You can find this process detailed in the section “Dealing with Underperformance on the Team” on page 216.)对于被标记为绩效不佳的人，你需要采取更亲力亲为的方式。共同制定一份有针对性的成长计划，解决其评估中指出的关键改进领域。（这一过程详见第 216 页“应对团队中的绩效不佳”一节。）

No matter the outcome, the performance review is just a milestone in a continuous process. What happens afterward is just as impactful as the review itself. The conversations you continue, the support you offer, and the plans you help shape will define how each team member grows and how your team moves forward together.

无论结果如何，绩效评估都只是一个持续过程中的里程碑。之后发生的事，与评估本身同样有影响力。你持续下去的谈话、你提供的支持、你帮着塑造的计划，将决定每位团队成员如何成长、以及你的团队如何共同前进。

Make Performance Reviews a Continuous Process让绩效评估成为持续的过程

Performance reviews don't start with the official announcement to “get your review ready,” and they certainly don't end with the final conversation about outcomes. A well-structured performance review happens all year long. Actually, the overwhelming nature of performance reviews comes from the fact that most people leave everything until the last minute: gathering feedback, compiling accomplishments, and preparing discussions.

绩效评估不是从那句“准备好你们的评估”的正式通知才开始的，当然也不是在那场关于结果的最后谈话就结束。结构良好的绩效评估贯穿全年。实际上，绩效评估之所以让人压力山大，正是因为大多数人把所有事都拖到最后一刻：收集反馈、整理成就、准备谈话。

— PDF p.223 —

But if you consistently track your accomplishments and challenges throughout the year, communicate them clearly to your manager, and use your one-on-ones effectively, to discuss goals, growth areas, and progress, then the actual review becomes a simple formality. By the time the review conversation happens, you should already have a clear idea of where you stand. And if something isn't possible, you should know well in advance rather than being caught off guard.

但如果你一整年都在持续跟踪自己的成就与挑战、清晰地向经理沟通、并有效利用一对一面谈来讨论目标、成长领域和进展，那么真正的评估就只是走个过场。等到评估谈话真的发生时，你应该早已清楚自己处于什么位置。而如果某件事不可能实现，你也应提前很久就知道，而不是被打个措手不及。

A simple trick I use, and one that everyone I've shared it with loves, is keeping a clear jar on my desk where I throw in colored Post-its with quick notes about things I'm proud of, milestones I've achieved, and challenges I've overcome. It's a low-effort way to track progress, and the visual reminder boosts confidence. Seeing the jar fill up over time serves as motivation, making it easier to recall accomplishments when review time comes.

我用一个简单的小窍门，而且每个我分享过的人都很喜欢：在桌上放一个透明罐子，往里扔彩色便利贴，随手记下我引以为豪的事、达成的里程碑、以及克服的挑战。这是一种低 effort 的跟踪进展方式，而看得见的提醒还能提升信心。看着罐子一天天被填满本身就是一种激励，也让评估季到来时更容易回忆起成就。

If you prefer digital tools, a simple Google Doc works just as well. The key is to choose a format that's easy to update and review regularly, something you'll actually use.

如果你更喜欢数字工具，一个简单的 Google Doc 也同样好用。关键是选一种容易更新、容易定期回顾、你真的会用的格式。

The next step is to apply this same approach to your team, tracking their progress continuously throughout the year. Keep notes on key accomplishments, challenges, and feedback from stakeholders. Then, when review time comes, you won't need to scramble for details; you can just review your notes and put together a clear, well-supported assessment. This approach saves time, reduces stress, and ensures that nothing important gets overlooked.

下一步就是把这套方法用到团队身上，全年持续跟踪他们的进展。记下关键成就、挑战和来自干系人的反馈。这样当评估季到来时，你就不必临时凑细节；只需回顾笔记、整理出一份清晰而有据可依的评估。这种做法省时、减压，并确保没有任何重要的东西被忽略。

This mindset should also extend to your team. If they regularly track their progress, performance reviews won't be a last-minute panic or a source of stress. There should be no surprises; people should already have a solid understanding of their strengths, areas for growth, and overall performance. A performance review should simply formalize what they already know.

这种心态也应延伸到团队。如果他们定期跟踪自己的进展，绩效评估就不会变成最后一刻的恐慌或压力之源。不该有意外；人们本就应该对自己的长处、成长领域和整体表现有扎实的理解。绩效评估只应把他们早已知道的东西正式化。

Yet, as we all know, this rarely happens. Too often, people react with “Oh no, not again” when review time rolls around. As a tech lead, it's on you to make sure performance reviews aren't just a rushed, once-a-year event but an ongoing habit. They should be on everyone's radar every day, with tracking accomplishments, setting milestones, and having a growth plan becoming second nature. Every one-on-one is a great opportunity to talk about their career growth and skill development.

然而，众所周知，这很少发生。太多时候，评估季一到，人们就“哦不，又来”。作为技术负责人，你有责任确保绩效评估不只是一年一次、匆匆忙忙的事件，而是一种持续的习惯。它应该每天都在每个人的雷达上，让跟踪成就、设定里程碑、拥有成长计划成为第二天性。每一次一对一面谈，都是谈论他们职业成长和技能发展的好机会。

The good news is that most companies support ongoing performance management with structured tools for tracking feedback, growth plans, and individual progress. These tools make it easy to navigate feedback over time, as they capture who shared it, when, what was said, and any resulting action points.

好消息是，大多数公司都用结构化工具支持持续的绩效管理，用来跟踪反馈、成长计划和个人进展。这些工具让你很容易跨越时间梳理反馈，因为它们记录了是谁分享的、何时、说了什么、以及由此产生的行动项。

As a tech lead, you'll often be the one ensuring that feedback is properly recorded and that it aligns with the expected format. It might feel like tedious admin work, but having structured, accessible records pays off, especially when it's time to write reviews, advocate for promotions, or support someone's development.

作为技术负责人，你常常要负责确保反馈被妥善记录、并符合期望的格式。这可能感觉像枯燥的行政活，但拥有结构化、易获取的记录是有回报的——尤其是在要写评估、为晋升发声、或支持某人发展的时候。

— PDF p.224 —

And as tech evolves, you may be able to offload some of that effort. For example, I know a tech lead who's experimenting with building an AI agent to input raw feedback into their internal tool, helping to save time while keeping everything organized. It's early days, but the idea of streamlining this kind of repetitive work is promising.

而随着技术演进，你也许能把一部分这类活外包出去。例如，我认识一位技术负责人，他正在试验构建一个 AI agent，把原始反馈录入内部工具，既省时又保持条理。虽然还在早期，但把这类重复性工作流水线化的想法很有前景。

Constantly thinking about performance, tracking it, and measuring progress helps not only to simplify reviews but also to refine how you assess growth and impact. Like any evolving practice, performance reviews should adapt based on feedback and experience. Find ways to make them more effective for both you and your team. The goal is to turn reviews into meaningful, growth-focused conversations rather than a once-a-year stress fest. Done right, they become a powerful tool for both personal and team development.

持续地思考绩效、跟踪绩效、衡量进展，不仅有助于简化评估，也有助于完善你评估成长与影响的方式。和任何不断演进的实践一样，绩效评估也应根据反馈和经验去调整。想办法让它对你和团队都更有效。目标是把评估变成有意义的、以成长为核心的对话，而不是一年一次的压力盛会。做对了，它会成为个人和团队发展的有力工具。

Common Challenges and How to Overcome Them常见挑战及应对方法

Stepping into the tech lead role often means facing a whole new set of responsibilities, many of which no one really prepares you for. Suddenly, you're expected to lead hiring processes, onboard new team members, run performance reviews, and shape the team culture. These are big, high-impact activities that affect the team's success, yet most tech leads are left to figure them out on their own.

走上技术负责人岗位，往往意味着面对一整套全新的职责，而其中很多根本没人真正教过你。突然间，你被期望主导招聘流程、帮新成员入职、主持绩效评估、并塑造团队文化。这些都是影响团队成败的重大、高影响活动，然而大多数技术负责人只能自己摸索。

Throughout this book, I've covered many of these responsibilities, but some challenges consistently stand out, either because they're hard to get right or because they're easy to overlook until they cause real problems.

在本书中，我已经讲过其中很多职责，但有几类挑战始终格外突出——要么因为它们很难做对，要么因为它们很容易被忽略、直到惹出真正的麻烦。

In this section, I'll walk you through three of the most common and critical challenges tech leads encounter when building and scaling teams:

在本节里，我会带你走过技术负责人在组建和扩展团队时最常见、也最关键的三大挑战：

  • Building an onboarding process from scratch从零搭建一套入职流程
  • Enabling collaboration by building trust and alignment inside the team通过在团队内部建立信任与对齐来促成协作
  • Dealing with underperformance, one of the toughest and most uncomfortable parts of leadership应对绩效不佳——这是领导力中最难、也最令人不适的部分之一

If you've never handled these before, that's completely normal. What matters is how you respond. This section gives you clear, actionable strategies to tackle these challenges head-on, and help your team grow stronger because of it.

如果你以前从未处理过这些，那完全正常。重要的是你如何应对。本节给你清晰、可执行的策略，让你正面迎接这些挑战，并让团队因此变得更强。

— PDF p.225 —

Building an Onboarding Process from Scratch从零搭建入职流程

If you're starting a team from scratch or don't have an onboarding process yet, here's a quick and easy way to put one in place with minimal effort the next time you hire someone new:

如果你正在从零组建团队、或还没有入职流程，下次招新人时，这里有一个简单易行、只需极少投入就能搭起一套流程的办法：

  1. Assign them a buddy, someone who can answer questions and guide them through the first few weeks.给他们配一位 buddy，一个能回答问题、在头几周引导他们的人。
  2. Ask them to document everything: the tools they use, the resources they find helpful, the challenges they face, and who they turn to for help.请他们把一切都记录下来：用到的工具、发现有帮助的资源、遇到的挑战、以及他们向谁求助。
  3. Review their notes to ensure accuracy and completeness.review 他们的笔记，确保准确和完整。
  4. Help them publish it as an internal guide for future hires.帮他们把它发布成一份供未来新人使用的内部指南。
  5. Give them credit! Recognizing their contribution makes them feel valued from day one.给他们记功！认可他们的贡献，让他们从第一天起就感到被重视。
  6. Ask each new hire to use and update the guide as they go through onboarding.请每一位新入职的人在经历入职时使用并更新这份指南。

That's it! You now have an onboarding process with minimal effort on your part, and the new hire gains early positive visibility within the team. This isn't the perfect onboarding process, but it's far better than having none. At the very least, your next new hire will have an easier time than the last.

就这么简单！你几乎没费什么力，就有了一套入职流程，而新人也在团队里早早获得了正面能见度。这不是一套完美的入职流程，但远胜于没有。至少，你的下一位新人会比上一位轻松些。

There is no such thing as a perfect onboarding process, but there are definitely bad ones. As a tech lead, your job is to be intentional about improving and adapting your onboarding process. A well-structured, continuously evolving onboarding experience directly contributes to team performance, helping new hires integrate faster, feel more confident, and become productive members of the team.

世上没有完美的入职流程，但确实有糟糕的入职流程。作为技术负责人，你的工作是有意识地改进和调整你的入职流程。一套结构良好、持续演进的入职体验，会直接助力团队绩效，帮新人更快融入、更自信、并成为团队中高效的一员。

Enabling Collaboration Inside the Team促进团队内部协作

We all know the benefits of proper collaboration, yet so many teams don't know how to work together effectively. Instead of complementing each other, sharing knowledge, and amplifying their collective impact, they end up getting in each other's way.

我们都知道良好协作的好处，然而太多团队并不知道如何高效共事。他们本应互补、共享知识、放大集体影响力，结果却互相碍事。

Some common symptoms:

一些常见症状：

  • Knowledge silos; everyone depends on specific people for critical pieces of work知识孤岛；做关键工作时每个人都得依赖某几个特定的人
  • Duplicated work; two people build the same thing, unaware of each other重复劳动；两个人做着同一件事，却互不知情
  • Time-wasting debates that go in circles and never lead to a clear decision兜圈子、浪费时间、却永远得不出清晰决策的争论
  • Lack of ownership; work bounces around with no clear driver缺乏担当；工作到处弹，没有明确的推动者
  • Reluctance to ask for help; people are afraid to look like they don't know羞于求助；人们害怕显得自己不懂
  • Decisions made in isolation, then revisited later because others weren't included在孤立中做出决策、又因当初没让其他人参与而事后重议
— PDF p.226 —

If any of this sounds familiar, you're not alone. The good news is there's a lot you can do as a tech lead to encourage collaboration by designing team processes that rely on interaction and shared ownership.

如果这些听着耳熟，你并不孤单。好消息是，作为技术负责人，你可以做很多事来鼓励协作——设计那些依赖互动和共同拥有的团队流程。

Pair programming结对编程

Pair programming is one of the simplest ways to build collaboration into your team's day-to-day work. Mix up pairs regularly to break down silos, spread knowledge, and create natural mentoring moments, especially between juniors and seniors. But don't frame it as a process to enforce. Instead, introduce it as a solution. For example, suggest two people work together to debug a tricky issue or design a complex flow. That's often how it sticks.

结对编程是把协作融入团队日常工作的最简单方式之一。定期打散结对，打破孤岛、传播知识、并创造自然的带教时刻，尤其是在初级者与资深者之间。但不要把它包装成一项要强制执行的制度。相反，把它作为一种解决方案引入。例如，建议两个人一起调试一个棘手问题、或设计一个复杂流程。它往往就是这样落地生根的。

That said, be aware that some people might resist it at first. On the surface, pair programming can feel like two people doing one person's job. It might seem inefficient, especially when deadlines are tight.

话虽如此，要意识到有些人一开始可能会抵触。表面上看，结对编程像是两个人干一个人的活。它可能显得低效，尤其是在截止日期紧张的时候。

But the real value shows up over time. Pairing reduces the time lost in context switching or transferring tasks when someone's sick or goes on vacation. It lowers the overall work in progress, helping people stay focused on finishing instead of just starting. It naturally creates a “four eyes” check, so you often don't need a separate PR review. And maybe most importantly, it speeds up onboarding, improves knowledge sharing, and builds collective code ownership across the team.

但真正的价值会随时间显现。结对减少了因上下文切换、或某人请假/度假而交接任务所浪费的时间。它降低了整体在制品量，帮人们专注于完成、而不只是开工。它天然形成“四眼”检查，因此往往不需要单独的 PR review。而也许最重要的是，它加快了入职、改善了知识共享、并在整个团队中建立起集体代码所有权。

Yes, there might be some short-term friction. But as a tech lead, you're thinking long term. Your goal is to help your team work more effectively together, and pairing is one of the most powerful habits to build that kind of culture, even if it takes some time to pay off and start seeing the benefits.

是的，短期可能会有些摩擦。但作为技术负责人，你要着眼长期。你的目标是帮团队更高效地协作，而结对正是建立这种文化最有力的习惯之一——哪怕它需要一段时间才能见效、开始显出好处。

Knowledge-sharing sessions知识分享会

There are a number of different ways to encourage knowledge sharing:

鼓励知识分享有很多不同的方式：

  • Run mob programming sessions to demo new libraries or frameworks.组织 mob programming（集体编程）环节，演示新的库或框架。
  • Host informal tech talks: no slides required, just show and tell.举办非正式的技术分享：不需要幻灯片，直接展示和讲解。
  • Make demos a shared responsibility: instead of running them yourself, assign them on the team board and rotate ownership.把演示变成共同的责任：不要自己全包，而是在团队看板上分派、并轮换负责人。
— PDF p.227 —

Support different styles; for example, some people prefer writing to speaking. Encourage those team members to write documentation, internal articles, or public blog posts (if there are no company restrictions).

支持不同的风格；例如，有些人更喜欢写而不是说。鼓励这些成员去写文档、内部文章、或公开的博客文章（如果公司没有限制的话）。

Onboarding as a team sport把入职当作团队运动

Onboarding is a great opportunity to get people to collaborate by simply using the buddy system and by making it a shared team process. This naturally gets people working together. See more ideas in the section “Involve the whole team” on page 176.

入职是一个让大家协作的好机会：只要用 buddy 制度、并把它变成团队共同的流程即可。这会自然地让人们一起共事。更多点子见第 176 页“让整个团队参与进来”一节。

Distribute responsibility分散责任

If you notice that a few people in your team are owning multiple initiatives or holding onto all the critical knowledge, it's time to step in. This kind of concentration of responsibility often leads to knowledge silos, burnout, and slowdowns when those individuals are unavailable. It also limits growth opportunities for others on the team. Encourage people to delegate and share ownership.

如果你注意到团队里有那么几个人同时扛着多个举措、或攥着全部关键知识，那就该介入了。这种责任的集中，往往会导致知识孤岛、倦怠，以及当这些人不在时的进度停滞。它还限制了团队里其他人的成长机会。鼓励人们授权、分享所有权。

Start by having open conversations with those who hold a lot of responsibility. Many times, they don't realize how much they're carrying or that it's actually blocking others from stepping up. Explain the broader benefits of delegation, both for the team and for themselves. For the team, it means learning, development, and stronger collaboration. For them, it means fewer context switches, less pressure, and possibly the freedom to take on something more exciting or strategic. You can frame it like this: “You've done a great job owning this area, and now that it's more stable, I think it's a great opportunity to bring someone else in to take over. That way, you can focus on that new initiative we discussed.”

先与那些扛着很多责任的人开诚布公地谈。很多时候，他们自己都没意识到扛了多少、也没意识到这其实挡住了别人站出来。向他们解释授权的更广泛好处——对团队和对他们自己都有。对团队，意味着学习、发展和更强的协作。对他们自己，意味着更少的上下文切换、更小的压力、以及或许能腾出手去做更激动人心或更具战略性的事。你可以这样来框定：“你把这块负责得很好，现在它更稳了，我觉得这是个好机会，带另一个人接手。这样你就能专心做我们之前聊的那个新举措。”

Make delegation feel like a growth opportunity, not a loss of control. Encourage them to mentor the person taking over. Ask them to document processes or walk others through the context. Make it clear that stepping back from ownership doesn't mean stepping away from impact; it just means their impact evolves.

让授权感觉像一次成长机会，而不是失去控制。鼓励他们带教接手的人。请他们把流程写成文档、或带别人过一遍背景。讲清楚：从“拥有”中退后一步，并不意味着从“影响力”中退出；只是意味着他们的影响力在演进。

Rotate facilitation roles. Don't let the same people always run retros, refine the backlog, or chase action items. Rotate those responsibilities to build shared ownership and reduce silent burnout.

轮换主持角色。不要总让同一批人主持复盘、梳理待办、或追着行动项跑。把这些责任轮换起来，以建立共同拥有、并减少默默的倦怠。

Pair people on initiatives在举措上为人们配对

One of the best ways to build confidence, accelerate growth, and encourage collaboration in your team is to pair people on initiatives, especially by giving less experienced engineers the lead, with a more senior person supporting them in the background as a “second chair.” This model works because it gives junior or mid-level team members real ownership while ensuring they're not left to figure everything out on their own. They get the chance to navigate ambiguity, make decisions, and present ideas, all with a safety net nearby.

在团队里建立信心、加速成长、鼓励协作的最好方式之一，就是在举措上为人们配对——尤其让经验较浅的工程师牵头，让一位更资深的人在幕后作为“第二席”支持他们。这种模式之所以有效，是因为它给了初级或中级成员真正的拥有权，同时确保他们不必独自摸索一切。他们有机会在附近有一张安全网的情况下，驾驭模糊、做决策、并呈现想法。

— PDF p.228 —

The key is to be crystal clear about the roles. Set expectations with the senior person up front: they're not there to take over or micromanage. Their role is to guide, mentor, and step in only when needed, allowing the less experienced lead to truly drive the work. Think of them like a copilot, alert and ready to support but not grabbing the wheel unless absolutely necessary.

关键是把角色讲得极其清楚。提前与资深者约定好期望：他们不是来接管或微观管理的。他们的角色是引导、带教、并只在需要时介入，让经验较浅的牵头者真正驱动工作。把他们想象成副驾驶：警觉、随时准备支持，但除非万不得已，不会去抢方向盘。

For example, let's say someone newer to the team wants to lead a cross-team integration project. Instead of handing it off to your most experienced engineer, flip the script. Have the newer person take point, leading meetings, managing timelines, and coordinating stakeholders, while the senior team member shadows, provides context, helps with tricky decisions, and acts as a sounding board behind the scenes.

例如，假设团队里一个较新的人想牵头一个跨团队的集成项目。不要把它交给你最资深的工程师，而是反过来。让这个较新的人打头阵：主持会议、管理时间线、协调干系人；而那位资深成员则在旁边跟随、提供背景、帮着做棘手决策、并在幕后充当回音板。

You should also make yourself available as a coach throughout the process. Encourage questions. Offer feedback. Help them navigate the process. Don't wait until something goes wrong; check in regularly to see how they're feeling and what support they need.

你自己也应在整个过程中随时扮演教练。鼓励提问、给出反馈、帮他们走通过程。不要等出了问题才动手；定期同步，看看他们感觉如何、需要什么支持。

Solve problems together一起解决问题

Solving problems as a team makes great team-building exercises.

作为一个团队一起解决问题，是绝佳的团队建设练习。

In one of my teams, we used to hold quick tech huddles after standup, gathering around a whiteboard to brainstorm solutions to tricky bugs or design challenges. No pressure, no formalities, just a space to throw around ideas and work things out together. These sessions helped us move faster, share knowledge, and stay aligned. The key is creating safety. Make it clear there are no bad ideas. Encourage everyone to speak up, even if they're unsure. Some of our best ideas started with “This might sound dumb, but what if…”

在我的一个团队里，我们常在站会后开一个简短的技术碰头会，围在白板旁，为棘手的 bug 或设计挑战 brainstorm 解决方案。没有压力、没有客套，只是一个抛想法、一起把事情捋清楚的空间。这些环节帮我们走得更快、共享知识、并保持对齐。关键是营造安全感。明确地说：没有坏主意。鼓励每个人都开口，哪怕自己也不确定。我们一些最好的想法，就是以“这听起来可能很蠢，但万一……”开头的。

Postmortems are another great example. Run them with a mindset of learning, not blame. If someone pushes broken code to production, don't ask, “Who messed up?” Ask, “Why did this happen, and how can we make recovery easier next time?” Maybe your pipeline is slow or you're missing feature flags. Focus on fixing the system, not blaming people.

复盘是另一个好例子。带着学习、而非追责的心态去开。如果有人把有问题的代码推到了生产，不要问“是谁搞砸了？”而要问“这件事为什么会发生？下次我们怎样才能让恢复更容易？”也许是你的流水线太慢，或缺少 feature flag。聚焦于修复系统，而不是责怪个人。

— PDF p.229 —

Premortems are also fun and useful. Before a risky launch, ask, “What could go wrong?” This surfaces hidden risks early and gets everyone thinking ahead.

事前验尸（premortem）也有趣又有用。在一次有风险的发布之前，问：“可能会出什么问题？”这会及早暴露隐藏的风险，并让每个人提前思考。

If you have to plan a new technical solution that will require architecture changes and impact multiple systems, instead of leaving it to one person to figure out the plan, use a collaborative process like a TD (technical definition) or RFC (request for comments). This involves drafting a shared document that outlines the proposed approach and sharing it with all relevant stakeholders: team members, other teams, architects, staff engineers, and anyone else who might be affected. This format gives everyone the opportunity to ask questions, raise concerns, and offer improvements before any decisions are finalized.

如果你要规划一个需要架构改动、并影响多个系统的新技术方案，不要把它丢给一个人去想计划，而是用一种协作流程，比如 TD（技术定义）或 RFC（意见征求书）。这包括起草一份共享文档，概述拟议的方案，并分享给所有相关干系人：团队成员、其他团队、架构师、staff 工程师、以及任何可能受影响的人。这种形式让每个人在决策敲定之前，都有机会提问、提出顾虑、并给出改进建议。

Whether it's huddles, postmortems, or premortems, the point is simple: shift from “your problem” to “our problem.” When teams solve things together, trust builds and collaboration becomes second nature.

无论是碰头会、复盘还是事前验尸，要点都很简单：从“你的问题”转向“我们的问题”。当团队一起解决问题时，信任就建立起来，协作也成为第二天性。

Celebrate together一起庆祝

Dealing with problems as a team is critical, but so is celebrating wins together, and doing it consistently. It sounds obvious, but many teams skip this step. They move from one milestone to the next without ever pausing to acknowledge what they've achieved.

作为一个团队一起应对问题固然关键，但一起、且持续地庆祝胜利同样关键。这听着理所当然，但很多团队就是跳过这一步。他们从一个里程碑奔向下一个里程碑，却从不停下来认可自己取得的成就。

I used to be guilty of this too. Focused on delivery and always thinking about the next thing, I'd often forget to take time to celebrate. Fortunately, I had someone on the team who didn't forget. They'd remind us to pause, schedule a lunch, set up a ping-pong match, or just take a moment to appreciate how far we'd come, even for small wins. And it made a huge difference. That energy carried into the work, strengthened our team bond, and made us more resilient during tough stretches.

我自己过去也曾在这上面犯过过错。一门心思扑在交付上、总想着下一件事，常常忘了花时间庆祝。幸运的是，团队里有人没忘。他们会提醒我们停一下，安排一顿午餐、组织一场乒乓赛，或只是花片刻欣赏我们走了多远——哪怕是小胜利。而这带来了巨大的不同。那股能量带进了工作、加固了团队的纽带、并让我们在艰难时段更有韧性。

Celebration doesn't have to be big or time-consuming. Start small: end the week with a “what we're proud of” round during standup or in Slack, or create a #shoutouts or #gratitude channel to recognize individual contributions. Use retrospectives not just to talk about what went wrong but also to highlight what went right. And don't just celebrate results; celebrate helpful behaviors. Call out mentoring, unblocking others, stepping up when needed, or simply supporting a team member.

庆祝不必大、也不必耗时。从小处做起：在站会或 Slack 里以一圈“我们引以为豪的事”结束一周，或建一个 #shoutouts 或 #gratitude 频道来认可个人贡献。用复盘不仅讨论哪里出了问题，也突出哪里做对了。而且不要只庆祝结果，也要庆祝助人的行为。点名表扬带教、为他人解除阻塞、在需要时站出来、或只是支持了某位团队成员。

— PDF p.230 —

Normalize asking for help让求助变得平常

One of the most effective leadership tools you have is vulnerability. Instead of expecting people to just do something, or demanding they do it, try asking for help.

你拥有的最有力的领导工具之一，就是脆弱。与其期望人们就把某件事做了、或命令他们做，不如试着请求帮助。

This approach can be especially powerful when working with strong personalities: people who seem resistant to everything, who challenge every decision, and who always push back.

在与个性强势的人打交道时，这种做法可能格外有力：那些似乎对一切都抵触、质疑每个决策、总是顶回来的人。

I once had a senior engineer who just would not get on board with a technical strategy the team had aligned on. I tried everything: walking through the pros and cons, looking for compromise, but nothing worked. He simply wouldn't budge. Meanwhile, I was under pressure from stakeholders to move forward. I didn't want to override him, so as a last resort, I tried something different. I got him into a one-on-one and said, “I'm going to be honest with you here. I really need you to get on board with this approach. I'm being pressured by stakeholders to make a decision today, and I'd really like to have you with us on this. I see your concerns, and the team is aware of them too. We're all willing to take on the risks together. So work with me here; what would it take for you to get on board?”

我曾有一位高级工程师，就是不肯认同团队已经对齐的一项技术策略。我什么办法都试过了：摆利弊、找折中，但都不管用。他就是寸步不让。与此同时，我承受着干系人要求推进的压力。我不想强行否决他，于是作为最后一招，我试了点不一样的。我把他约进一对一面谈，说：“我跟你说实话。我真的需要你在这件事上跟我们站在一起。干系人压着我今天就要做决定，而我真的很希望你能加入我们。我看到了你的顾虑，团队也知道。我们都愿意共同承担风险。所以，请和我一起；要怎样你才愿意上车？”

That conversation changed everything. He replied, “Thank you for sharing this with me. I didn't realize the pressure you were under or how much I was blocking progress. I'm OK moving forward with the team's decision. I'd just like to write down my concerns in case things go wrong so we have my ideas documented,” which I readily agreed to.

那场谈话改变了一切。他回答：“谢谢你告诉我这些。我没意识到你承受的压力，也没意识到自己挡住了多少进展。我可以接受按团队的决定推进。我只是想把我的顾虑写下来，以防万一出问题，也好把我的想法留个记录。”我当即欣然同意。

That moment was a turning point for me as a leader. It showed me that asking for help, even from someone who disagrees with you, can shift the dynamic completely. It's not easy. It requires vulnerability, humility, and getting out of your comfort zone. But once I started doing it, everything changed. I saw my team jump in and take things off my plate without hesitation. When I admitted I was overwhelmed, or unsure, they didn't judge; they supported. And not just because they had to but because they wanted to. All I had to do was name the thing I was struggling with and ask.

那一刻是我作为领导者的转折点。它让我看到：请求帮助——哪怕是向一个与你意见相左的人——也能彻底改变局面。这并不容易。它需要脆弱、谦逊、以及走出舒适区。但一旦我开始这么做，一切都变了。我看到团队毫不犹豫地跳进来、替我分担。当我承认自己扛不住、或没把握时，他们没有评判，而是支持。而且不只是因为他们不得不，而是因为他们愿意。我所要做的，只是说出我正挣扎的那件事、然后开口请求。

Once I experienced that kind of support, I couldn't go back.

一旦我体验过那种支持，就再也回不去了。

So if you're facing resistance or feeling stuck, try asking for help. Not as a tactic but as a genuine invitation. You might be surprised by how much it changes the conversation and the relationship.

所以，如果你正面对抵触、或感到卡住，试着请求帮助。不是当作一种话术，而是作为一次真诚的邀请。你可能会惊讶于它给对话和关系带来的改变。

— PDF p.231 —

Make information transparent and visible to everyone让信息对所有人透明、可见

If you want people to take ownership and collaborate effectively, they need access to the right information, without having to dig for it or ask around. Transparency builds trust, reduces misunderstandings, and empowers your team to take initiative.

如果你希望人们担起责任、高效协作，他们就需要接触到正确的信息——而不必自己去翻、去到处问。透明建立信任、减少误解、并赋能团队主动行动。

Start by creating shared documentation spaces where everyone can track progress, processes, and decisions. Whether it's a project board, a shared roadmap, or a simple team wiki, make sure it's easy to find, easy to update, and actually used.

先创建共享的文档空间，让每个人都能跟踪进展、流程和决策。无论是项目看板、共享路线图、还是一个简单的团队 wiki，都要确保它容易找到、容易更新、并且真的有人用。

Before kicking off new projects, run short alignment check-ins. Use these to clarify expectations, constraints, roles, and responsibilities. It's a simple habit that prevents weeks of confusion later. When people know what's happening and why, they're more likely to contribute ideas, ask smart questions, and challenge things that don't make sense.

在启动新项目之前，开一个简短的对齐会。用它澄清期望、约束、角色和责任。这是一个简单的习惯，却能避免日后数周的混乱。当人们知道正在发生什么、以及为什么时，他们更可能贡献想法、提出聪明的问题、并质疑那些说不通的事。

The more context you give your team, the more ownership they'll take.

你给团队的上下文越多，他们承担的拥有感就越强。

You can find more information on this topic in the section “Be Transparent in Your Communication” on page 67.

关于这个话题，更多内容见第 67 页“沟通要透明”一节。

Some of these approaches may take time to stick. Yes, pairing might feel inefficient at first. Delegating might slow things down short-term. But these are long-term investments. You're building a team that shares ownership, adapts faster, and grows together.

这些做法中有一些可能需要时间才能扎根。是的，结对起初可能显得低效。授权短期可能拖慢进度。但这些都是长期投资。你在建设一个共同拥有、适应更快、共同成长的团队。

And remember, just because you create opportunities for collaboration doesn't mean people will use them right away. You need to lead by example. Use the practices yourself, talk about why they matter, and bring people along one step at a time. Not everything will work for your team, and that's OK. Try, adapt, and learn.

还要记住：你创造了协作机会，并不意味着人们立刻就会用。你需要以身作则。自己先用这些做法，讲讲它们为什么重要，一步一步带人跟上。不是每种做法都适合你的团队，而这没关系。尝试、调整、学习。

Hopefully, some of the techniques shared here will start to gain traction with your team, but in my experience, if those efforts aren't sticking, it's often because they're bumping up against bigger, underlying problems in the team's foundation. Two of the most common root causes are lack of psychological safety and unclear ways of working.

希望这里分享的一些技巧能在你的团队里开始奏效；但根据我的经验，如果这些努力落不了地，往往是因为它们撞上了团队基础中更大、更深层的问题。两个最常见的根因是：缺乏心理安全感，以及不清晰的工作方式。

Lack of psychological safety is one of the biggest silent blockers to collaboration. When people are afraid of being blamed, judged, or seen as incompetent, they stop speaking up. They hold back ideas because they're afraid they'll sound stupid. They don't ask for help because they think it will make them look weak. They don't admit when they've made a mistake because they're afraid of the consequences.

缺乏心理安全感，是协作最大的隐性障碍之一。当人们害怕被责怪、被评判、或被看作无能时，他们就会停止发声。他们憋着想法，因为怕显得蠢。他们不求助，因为觉得那会显得自己弱。他们不承认自己犯了错，因为害怕后果。

— PDF p.232 —

So instead of open conversation, you get silence. Instead of learning from mistakes, you get cover-ups. And instead of collaboration, you get isolation. You can run all the retros, tech huddles, and pairing sessions in the world, but if people don't feel safe to be honest, those rituals won't work the way they're supposed to.

于是，你得到的不是开放对话，而是沉默；不是从错误中学习，而是遮掩；不是协作，而是孤立。你可以开遍天下所有的复盘、技术碰头和结对环节，但如果人们不感到可以诚实地表达，这些仪式就不会按预期起效。

The second silent killer of collaboration is when the team doesn't have a shared understanding of how to work together. Everyone assumes they know what “good” looks like, but everyone has a different version. This leads to confusion around roles, ownership, and decision making. Tasks fall through the cracks, handoffs are messy, and accountability is vague. People step on each other's toes or, worse, avoid taking initiative because they're not sure it's their responsibility. You end up with the classic case of “everyone owns it, so no one does.”

协作的第二个隐性杀手，是团队对“如何协作”缺乏共同理解。每个人都以为自己知道“好”长什么样，但每个人心里的版本都不一样。这会导致在角色、拥有权和决策上的混乱。任务掉缝里、交接一团糟、责任模糊。人们互相踩脚，或更糟——因为不确定是不是自己的责任而避免主动。你最终会落到那个经典困境：“人人都负责，所以没人负责。”

To dig deeper and address those root issues, I recommend checking out the section “How to Build a Healthy Team Culture” on page 185 and the section “How to Create Psychological Safety on Your Team” on page 188. That's where real, long-lasting change starts.

要深挖并解决这些根因，我建议去读第 185 页“如何打造健康的团队文化”一节，以及第 188 页“如何在团队中建立心理安全感”一节。真正、持久的改变，从那里开始。

Dealing with Underperformance on the Team应对团队中的绩效不佳

One of the hardest and most uncomfortable responsibilities of being a tech lead is dealing with underperformance. Because it's uncomfortable and hard to navigate, most tech leads just avoid it. They wait too long or miss the opportunity to prevent the situation altogether by not setting clear expectations early on.

作为技术负责人最难、也最令人不适的职责之一，就是应对绩效不佳。因为它令人不适、又难以拿捏，大多数技术负责人干脆避而不谈。他们等得太久，或因为没有早早设定清晰期望，而错失了从根本上预防这种局面的机会。

Most of the time, when someone isn't meeting expectations, it's not because they're lazy or incapable, it's because expectations were never clearly set in the first place. We assume people know what we expect from them without actually saying it out loud.

大多数时候，某人之所以未达期望，并不是因为他懒惰或无能，而是因为期望从一开始就没被清晰地设定过。我们默认人们知道我们对他们的期望，却从未真正把它说出口。

So the first thing you should do is make sure every team member has a clear understanding of what's expected in their role. Use your one-on-ones to ask them to review the job description. Follow up on any questions or confusion. Just getting through that list once can eliminate “I didn't know” as a reason for underperformance. You don't want to end up in a conversation where someone says, “I didn't know you expected me to mentor others.” That's a harder conversation than it needs to be.

因此，你要做的第一件事，是确保每位团队成员都清楚自己岗位上的期望。利用一对一面谈，请他们过一遍岗位描述。跟进任何疑问或困惑。光是把那张清单过一遍，就能消除“我不知道”这个绩效不佳的借口。你不会想落到这样一场对话里：有人说“我根本不知道你还期望我去带教别人。”那会让这场谈话变得比它本应有的更难。

The second thing: act fast when you see an issue. One common mistake tech leads make is waiting too long. You notice a problem; maybe someone is consistently missing deliverables or they're not as “strong” as you expected, but you hold off saying anything. And the longer you wait, the bigger the problem gets.

第二件事：一发现问题就迅速行动。技术负责人常犯的一个错，就是等太久。你注意到一个问题——也许某人总是交不出交付物、或没有你预期的那么“强”——但你憋着不说。而你等得越久，问题就越大。

— PDF p.233 —

So as soon as you notice something, bring it up. It might be something they're not aware of, or maybe you haven't been super clear about what “good” looks like. If someone is supposed to be involved in interviews but keeps skipping them, ask them why. Is it because they don't know it's expected? Or maybe they're unsure how to do it and need help.

所以一注意到什么，就提出来。那可能是他们自己没意识到的事，也可能是你对“好”长什么样一直没讲得很清楚。如果某人本该参与面试、却老是缺席，就问问他为什么。是因为他不知道这是期望中的事？还是他不确定怎么做、需要帮助？

Sometimes it's smaller stuff, like communication. Maybe someone leading a team initiative isn't responding to questions from other teams on Slack on the subject. You assume it's obvious they should, but have you ever actually said it out loud? Have you told them that responsiveness is part of leading an initiative? A quick conversation can clear that up.

有时是些更小的事，比如沟通。也许某个牵头团队举措的人，没有在 Slack 上回应其他团队就该事项提出的问题。你以为这是不言自明的，但你真的说出口过吗？你告诉过他们“及时响应”是牵头一个举措的一部分吗？一次简短的谈话就能把它讲清楚。

Whatever it is, give feedback fast. The value of feedback drops the longer you wait, especially when it's about something that needs improvement. If you feel like someone is struggling across multiple areas, go back to the expectations and talk through where the gaps are.

无论是什么，都尽快给反馈。反馈的价值会随等待时间衰减，尤其是当它关乎需要改进的地方时。如果你觉得某人在多个领域都吃力，就回到期望上，一起把缺口在哪里谈清楚。

I've seen a lot of tech leads put off these tough conversations, thinking they'll wait until the next performance review. But that's usually months away, and by then, it's too late. Telling someone “You could have handled that client call better… six months ago” just doesn't help. It's not actionable anymore; it just feels like blame. And that kind of delay can mess with someone's career path. A simple, timely bit of feedback early on could've helped them course-correct before things got worse.

我见过很多技术负责人把这些艰难的谈话一拖再拖，想着等到下一次绩效评估再说。但那通常是几个月后，而到那时已经太晚了。对某人说“那通客户电话你本可以处理得更好……六个月前”，根本无济于事。它已经不可执行了，只让人觉得是在指责。而这种拖延会搞砸一个人的职业道路。一句简单、及时、早早给出的反馈，本可以在事情变糟之前帮他纠正方向。

Let's say you've been quietly hoping someone improves their code quality. You hint at it in retros with comments like “We need to get better at testing,” but nothing changes. Fast forward a few months, and now you're having a hard conversation: “Your work keeps coming back from QA with bugs. We need to talk about a performance improvement plan.” At that point, they're blindsided, and honestly, they're not wrong to be. A simple, specific conversation early on could've made a huge difference. I've seen people completely turn things around after one honest and well-timed piece of feedback.

假设你一直在心里默默希望某人提升代码质量。你在复盘里用“我们得在测试上做得更好”这类话旁敲侧击，但毫无改变。几个月后，你们开始一场艰难的谈话：“你的活总是带着 bug 被 QA 打回来。我们得谈谈绩效改进计划了。”这时他们被打了个措手不及，而且说实话，他们有理由如此。早早来一次简单、具体的谈话，本可以带来巨大不同。我见过有人在一次诚实而及时的反馈之后，彻底扭转了局面。

Supporting someone's growth, especially when performance is falling short, can be a complex and emotionally demanding process. That's why you shouldn't do it alone. If you're seeing persistent issues or if it's unclear how to proceed, involve your engineering manager, HR, or the people team early. Managing underperformance often comes with legal and procedural implications, things that are completely out of your control and outside your responsibilities.

支持一个人的成长——尤其是当绩效不达标的时候——可能是一个复杂、且耗费情绪的过程。这就是为什么你不该独自承担。如果你看到持续性的问题、或不清楚该如何推进，就尽早让工程经理、HR 或人事团队介入。管理绩效不佳往往牵涉法律和流程上的事项，那些完全超出你的掌控、也不在你的职责范围内。

— PDF p.234 —

Before taking any action, make sure all the people involved agree there's a challenge worth addressing. This includes you, the person in question, and the rest of the people involved mentioned before.

在采取任何行动之前，确保所有相关方都同意存在一个值得解决的挑战。这包括你、当事人，以及前面提到的其他相关人员。

Once there's alignment that something needs attention, you can jump in to help from your role. This isn't about creating a formal performance improvement plan, which is typically owned by HR or the EM, but rather cocreating a practical, supportive plan to help someone improve. You are the closest to this team member in the day-to-day, so you are in the best position to help them shape a growth plan and take action.

一旦大家对齐“某件事需要被关注”，你就可以从自己的角色切入帮忙。这不是要去制定一份正式的绩效改进计划——那通常由 HR 或工程经理负责——而是共同制定一份务实、支持性的计划来帮人改进。你是日常中离这位团队成员最近的人，因此你最有条件帮他塑造成长计划、并采取行动。
